articles.title: Como sobrevivi a uma explosao que deixou 650 mortos: 'As cortinas grudaram no teto' | G1
articles.standfirst: Virginia Martínez Tellez é uma das sobreviventes de um dos desastres industriais mais graves da história. Um vazamento de gás em um depósito da petroleira Pemex mudaria para sempre a sua vida, a de sua família e a de toda uma comunidade.
articles.summary: Virginia Martínez Tellez é uma das sobreviventes de um dos desastres industriais mais graves da história. Um vazamento de gás em um depósito da petroleira Pemex mudaria para sempre a sua vida, a de sua família e a de toda uma comunidade.
articles.body:
Eram 5h30 da manhã de 19 de novembro de 1984. Virginia Martínez Téllez, de 13 anos, dormia ao lado de sua família em San Juan Ixhuatepec, hoje popularmente conhecido como San Juanico, um subúrbio ao norte da Cidade do México.

Nem ela nem os cerca de 40 mil outros habitantes do local, que vivem em casas construídas em sua maioria de concreto e madeira, perceberam um enorme vazamento de gás que mudaria suas vidas para sempre.

A jovem vivia a aproximadamente um quilômetro de uma instalação de armazenamento e distribuição de gás pertencente à Pemex, a petrolífera estatal do México.

Por isso, estava acostumada a ver a chama da tocha de queima, onde o excesso de gás é incinerado, acesa 24 horas por dia. Fazia parte da paisagem cotidiana. Mas o que veria ao acordar naquela madrugada seria algo completamente diferente.

"Parecia uma zona de guerra", recorda ela, em entrevista ao programa Witness History, da BBC.

O episódio, que ficou conhecido como desastre de San Juanico, deixou mais de 650 mortos e 2.500 feridos, além de cerca de 25 mil pessoas desabrigadas.

Virginia morava com seus seis irmãos, a avó e os pais. "Era uma comunidade de pessoas muito trabalhadoras e com recursos limitados, de classe média baixa", conta ela.

Ela estava prestes a completar 14 anos quando ocorreu o desastre, que se tornaria a explosão de gás mais mortal do México e do mundo.

Nas duas décadas anteriores, os bairros de San Juanico haviam crescido consideravelmente, de modo que algumas casas ficavam a apenas 130 metros da instalação.

O complexo contava com seis enormes tanques esféricos de armazenamento e dezenas de reservatórios cilíndricos, popularmente conhecidos como "salsichas".

Tudo isso seria reduzido a pedaços naquela madrugada.

"Foi uma explosão muito forte. Levantei da cama e vi que as cortinas estavam grudadas no teto, como se fossem a saia de Marilyn Monroe levantada pelo vento", recorda Virginia.

"Olhei imediatamente para fora e tudo estava alaranjado, com tons azulados e formas que pareciam línguas de fogo. Lembro-me da luz, do barulho, do caos. Um calor avassalador e o terror de pensar que, a qualquer momento, tudo poderia explodir novamente", relata.

O vazamento de gás em um dos reservatórios formou uma nuvem de vapor. A nuvem pegou fogo, provocando uma labareda e uma explosão.

O incêndio se espalhou a partir de um caminhão-tanque que explodiu, desencadeando uma reação em cadeia nas instalações de armazenamento, cujos reservatórios normalmente continham 80 mil barris de gás liquefeito.

Pouco antes do amanhecer, uma coluna de fogo se elevou a mais de um quilômetro e meio no céu noturno, cobrindo aquele subúrbio de moradias precárias com uma chuva de destroços em chamas.

"Havia um enorme redemoinho, no qual voavam inúmeras partículas. Pareciam chapas de metal", recorda Virginia.

Segundo relatos, o clarão avermelhado podia ser visto do outro extremo da capital.

Virginia sentia o ar se comprimir dentro de seu quarto. "É como quando você mergulha debaixo d'água: quanto mais fundo desce, maior é a pressão que sente."

"Levantem-se, vamos! Temos que ir embora! Calcem os sapatos, os primeiros que encontrarem!", disse a mãe de Virginia aos filhos naquela madrugada.

"Meu pai tentou abrir a porta, mas, assim que tocou na maçaneta de metal, queimou a mão. Ele precisou usar um pano para se proteger e conseguir abrir a porta de casa."

Quando conseguiram sair, sentiram um calor abrasador. Muitos vizinhos tentavam escapar descalços e de roupa íntima. Toda a família correu em direção ao que esperava ser sua salvação diante do fogo e da radiação térmica: seu velho carro, que precisava ser empurrado para pegar.

Todos se apertaram dentro do veículo. O pai dirigia em meio a uma névoa de fumaça, mas as obras de construção e pavimentação tornavam as estradas ainda mais difíceis de atravessar.

Virginia olhava pela janela. "Havia um caos imenso. Pessoas correndo, gritando, subindo a colina como formigas. Elas se dirigiam ao morro Zacatenco para chegar ao então Distrito Federal. Tudo estava acinzentado, muito escuro, como se houvesse uma neblina espessa. Suponho que fossem os resíduos da primeira explosão", ela recorda.

Em seguida, pegaram a rodovia México-Pachuca em direção a Indios Verdes e, a aproximadamente um quilômetro de San Juanico, ocorreu a segunda explosão.

"Ouvi o estrondo. Olhei para trás e vi uma coluna de fogo gigantesca, enorme. Fiquei com muito medo de que San Juanico já não existisse mais."

O fogo permaneceu fora de controle durante sete horas.

"Eu era a terceira de sete irmãos. Tinha duas irmãs mais velhas. Elas tentavam nos consolar e nos abraçar. Nós, por nossa vez, tentávamos tranquilizar e controlar os mais novos", conta Virginia.

"Meus pais, é claro, também estavam aterrorizados, mas meu pai manteve a calma para garantir nossa segurança e nos tirar dali o mais rápido possível."

Novas explosões ocorreram, conhecidas como BLEVE (explosões decorrentes da expansão de vapores pela ebulição de líquidos), à medida que outros tanques de armazenamento se rompiam.

Enquanto Virginia e sua família fugiam em direção à zona leste da Cidade do México, milhares de profissionais de emergência seguiam rumo ao epicentro do desastre.

Ao longo de todo o dia, três mil policiais, com o apoio de soldados e voluntários da Cruz Vermelha, resgataram um número cada vez maior de vítimas em meio aos escombros. Os serviços médicos da cidade ficaram sobrecarregados.

A família chegou em segurança à casa de parentes e acompanhou horrorizada as notícias na televisão, enquanto a dimensão da devastação era revelada.

"Havia crianças perdidas, pessoas separadas de suas famílias e outras que não conseguiram escapar e permaneceram abraçadas umas às outras", afirma Virginia.

Sua família queria voltar para casa, mas não era tão simples.

"Era uma cidade fantasma, isolada por cordões de segurança. O Exército mexicano não nos deixava entrar. Meu pai, acompanhado de alguns sobrinhos, conseguiu entrar primeiro. Depois soube que eles haviam subornado alguns guardas. Assim, conseguiram entrar a pé para alimentar os animais de estimação que tinham ficado em casa", recorda.

Eles foram os primeiros a ver toda a desolação que havia no local.

Virginia só voltou em dezembro. A casa de sua infância havia se transformado em um cenário de pesadelo. Duas valas comuns foram abertas para enterrar centenas de vítimas.

"Foi muito triste. Algo dentro de mim se rompeu. Compreendi a dimensão do desastre. Parecia uma zona de guerra. Havia um cheiro que, até hoje, não consigo descrever. Era algo completamente diferente. Meus pais diziam que cheirava a carne queimada."

Também havia sinais visíveis do calor extremo e da força das explosões sucessivas que devastaram o bairro. Um dos tanques de armazenamento foi arremessado a quatro quarteirões de distância.

"Vi casas destruídas ao longo do Rio de los Remedios, residências que pertenciam a colegas de escola", conta. "Também olhei para a colina e vi onde os projéteis haviam caído. Fragmentos das esferas de armazenamento ou daqueles recipientes compridos que chamávamos de 'salsichas' tinham caído sobre as casas."

A Pemex assumiu a responsabilidade pelo desastre e concordou em indenizar as vítimas.

Especialistas em saúde e segurança concluíram que a tragédia foi resultado de uma combinação de falhas técnicas, deficiências nos sistemas de segurança e planejamento urbano inadequado.

Para Virginia, a explosão de San Juanico continua afetando sua vida mais de 40 anos depois:

"Sou extremamente sensível ao cheiro de gás. Fico muito agitada e em estado de alerta máximo quando acontece algo parecido", conta. "Isso me afeta profundamente. Na verdade, desenvolvi uma espécie de ansiedade, o que hoje chamaríamos de transtorno de estresse pós-traumático."

Infelizmente, aquela não foi a única explosão envolvendo a petrolífera estatal mexicana.

Acidentes industriais semelhantes ocorreram em outras localidades do país, como Guadalajara, Reynosa, San Martín Texmelucan, Coatzacoalcos e Tlahuelilpan.

Mas a tragédia de San Juanico continua sendo a mais mortal.

*Com informações do podcast Witness History, da BBC

articles.title: Dupla italiana: aprenda a preparar focaccia e caponata  | G1
articles.standfirst: Clássicos da culinária italiana têm preparo fácil.
articles.summary: Clássicos da culinária italiana têm preparo fácil.
articles.body:
A herança italiana se faz muito presente na gastronomia do Paraná - e vai muito além das massas e queijos. O Caminhos do Campo mostra o preparo de dois clássicos italianos que combinam com o café da tarde ou como entradas para refeições maiores: focaccia e caponata. Quem ensina é o chefe Alisson Badiluk, de Pato Branco , no sudoeste do estado.

2 berinjelas médias (podem ser substituídas por abobrinha);

Sal, pimenta-do-reino e pimenta calabresa a gosto;

Comece aquecendo bem uma frigideira ou panela grande. Adicione um fio generoso de azeite e doure a berinjela cortada em cubos. A dica é dourar em pequenas porções, para não soltar tanta água. Depois de dois minutos no fogo, reserve em uma travessa.

Adicione novamente um fio de azeite e refogue a cebola e o pimentão picados.

Após estes ingredientes ficarem macios, acrescente o tomate picado e refogue por alguns minutinhos. Uma dica é não cozinhar muito para não desmanchar.

Acrescente as nozes, alcaparra, pimenta-calabresa e azeitonas, e misture.

Adicione a berinjela que estava reservada e tempere tudo com sal e pimenta a gosto.

Acrescente as uvas passas brancas, marinadas ao vinho tinto.

Adicione o mel e finalize com folhas de manjericão e raspas de limão siciliano.

Comece misturando a farinha com açúcar, fermento e adicione água, na batedeira.

Em seguida adicione o sal e azeite para a massa ficar homogênea. Bata até incorporar.

Cubra a massa e aguarde cerca de 30 minutos até ela dobrar se tamanho. Depois, é só transferi-la para uma forma untada.

Para ajudar a espalhar a massa e criar cavidades para adicionar o recheio, umedeça a ponta dos dedos com azeite de oliva e pressione gentilmente a massa, abrindo levemente em direção à borda da forma.

Regue a massa com azeite de oliva e adicione o sal e alecrim, além do tomate cereja.

Leve para assar em forno pré-aquecido a 220°C por 20 a 30 minutos, até dourar.

articles.title: Tatuagem vai de arte surrealista e a tradição japonesa em Sorocaba | G1
articles.standfirst: Fernanda Paiva aposta no surrealismo para transformar animais em personagens de situações improváveis enquanto Vinicius Maciel explora a riqueza estética e cultural da tatuagem tradicional japonesa em Sorocaba (SP).
articles.summary: Artistas de tatuagem em Sorocaba (SP) utilizam o surrealismo e a cultura japonesa para transformar animais e memórias em desenhos únicos e fora do convencional.
articles.body:
🐸🐢🐈 Um sapo vestido com trajes elegantes, uma tartaruga envolvida em uma briga no fundo do mar ou um gato inserido em uma composição inspirada na arte japonesa. Na pele, nem tudo precisa seguir o caminho dos desenhos convencionais. Em Sorocaba (SP), artistas têm explorado diferentes possibilidades da tatuagem para transformar ideias inusitadas e referências artísticas em trabalhos que fogem do comum. Assista o vídeo acima.

É o caso da tatuadora Fernanda Paiva, de 28 anos, que encontrou no surrealismo a identidade do seu trabalho, e de Vinicius Maciel, de 33, que se dedica à tatuagem tradicional japonesa e utiliza elementos da cultura oriental para desenvolver suas composições.

Embora sigam caminhos artísticos diferentes, os dois têm algo em comum: a preocupação em construir trabalhos que vão além da reprodução de imagens e carregam características próprias de seus universos criativos.

Fernanda Paiva trabalha com desenhos surrealistas — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

A trajetória de Fernanda na tatuagem começou depois de uma mudança de planos. Apesar de desenhar desde criança, ela chegou a ingressar na faculdade de medicina veterinária aos 18 anos. Durante a graduação, porém, percebeu que não se identificava com a profissão.

A decisão de mudar de caminho veio durante a pandemia, quando cursava o quarto ano e enfrentava um período de esgotamento mental. Foi quando optou por trancar o curso e investir no universo artístico.

Com a ajuda de um amigo tatuador, que a aproximou de materiais e referências da profissão, começou a estudar por conta própria. Aprendeu por meio de vídeos na internet e passou um período treinando em pele artificial antes de começar a tatuar pessoas.

Hoje, o surrealismo é a principal definição de seu trabalho. A artista utiliza animais como protagonistas de situações que dificilmente seriam encontradas na natureza, explorando o absurdo e a imaginação.

“Sempre tive uma afinidade muito grande com animais, mas gosto de explorá-los para além da representação naturalista, imaginando situações, criaturas e comportamentos que não encontraríamos na natureza”, explica.

A proposta aparece até mesmo na maneira como ela descreve suas criações: “Aqui um sapo pode vestir trajes elegantes e uma tartaruga pode quebrar o braço numa rinha no fundo do oceano”.

Um sapo pode vestir trajes elegantes e uma tartaruga pode quebrar o braço numa rinha no fundo do oceano — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

A construção da identidade surrealista, entretanto, não aconteceu por acaso. Antes de desenvolver uma linguagem própria, Fernanda estudou obras de grandes nomes do surrealismo, como René Magritte e Max Ernst. A reprodução dessas referências, feita durante seus estudos e sem finalidade comercial, ajudou a reconhecer os elementos com os quais mais tinha afinidade artisticamente.

A partir daí, passou a desenvolver um universo próprio, sem a intenção de oferecer diferentes estilos de tatuagem. “Não tenho interesse em oferecer um catálogo de estilos diferentes, prefiro aprofundar e desenvolver cada vez mais o universo que estou construindo”, afirma.

Parte desse processo também aconteceu longe da máquina de tatuagem. Fernanda mantém um caderno chamado “caderno de tudo” , no qual registra ideias que surgem das mais diferentes situações, desde referências artísticas até conversas informais.

Filmes de animação, stop motion, quadrinhos, músicas e acontecimentos cotidianos também alimentam sua criatividade. Às vezes, uma ideia aparentemente sem sentido pode se transformar em um desenho.

Além das ilustrações criadas a partir da própria imaginação, a tatuadora desenvolve projetos personalizados, especialmente retratos de animais de estimação. Nesse caso, os bichinhos podem ganhar características inesperadas e protagonizar pequenas aventuras que representam suas personalidades.

“Imagina ter seu animal de estimação eternizado de uma maneira completamente inusitada? Ele pode aparecer praticando alguma atividade improvável, vivendo uma pequena aventura ou protagonizando uma situação que representa sua personalidade”, conta.

Trabalhos autorais da Fernanda Paiva — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Uma das tatuagens mais marcantes de sua trajetória surgiu justamente de uma proposta personalizada. Um cliente que conheceu na faculdade de veterinária procurou Fernanda para reformular uma pequena tatuagem de carneiro que tinha no braço. Como referências obrigatórias, apresentou apenas dois elementos: um macaco-de-cheiro e lírios.

Depois de algumas tentativas, a ideia ganhou um novo rumo quando o cliente sugeriu que o macaco aparecesse usando pijama. A partir dessa mudança, a artista desenvolveu uma composição com atmosfera de sonho, incluindo nuvens e carneirinhos pulando.

O detalhe curioso veio somente no fim da sessão: o macaco fazia referência a uma música de ninar da infância do cliente. Sem conhecer previamente a história, Fernanda havia desenvolvido uma ilustração que acabou dialogando diretamente com a memória pessoal dele.

Para a tatuadora, essa troca entre artista e cliente é uma das partes mais interessantes do processo. Mais do que reproduzir uma imagem apresentada, ela procura interpretar histórias e referências para transformá-las em algo que também carregue sua identidade.

Detalhes da tatuagem que teve como referências o macaco-de-cheiro, carneiros e lírios — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Vinicius Maciel tatua há 14 anos — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Se Fernanda encontra inspiração no absurdo e na liberdade de imaginar situações improváveis, Vinicius Maciel segue um caminho que passa pela história e pela tradição artística japonesa.

Natural de Iperó (SP), onde cresceu, o tatuador começou na profissão em 2012. Seu interesse pela tatuagem surgiu ainda antes, influenciado principalmente pelos integrantes de bandas que acompanha até hoje.

No início, a intenção era conseguir fazer tatuagens na própria pele e nos amigos. Ele chegou a comprar um kit de tatuagem, mas logo percebeu que o trabalho exigia muito mais do que imaginava.

“Por mais que não tivesse acesso a entender a mecânica e técnicas da profissão, o interesse e a curiosidade foram aumentando e, consequentemente, a paixão nasceu ao conhecer o mundo da tatuagem e sua cultura”, relembra.

Ao longo de 14 anos de profissão, passou por diferentes estilos, desde trabalhos mais comerciais até vertentes tradicionais, como old school e chicano. Atualmente, encontrou na tatuagem japonesa uma forma de aprofundar seus estudos e desenvolver uma linguagem com a qual já tinha afinidade.

A estética é inspirada em referências históricas, como o ukiyo-e, técnica de xilogravura japonesa popular durante o período Edo. Entre os artistas que influenciam seu trabalho estão Katsushika Hokusai e Utagawa Kuniyoshi.

Dentro desse universo, os gatos também se tornaram personagens frequentes das suas criações. A presença desses animais em contos e pinturas da cultura japonesa despertou no tatuador a possibilidade de explorar diferentes representações, combinando a figura felina com os elementos da estética oriental.

Mas a tatuagem tradicional japonesa vai muito além da escolha dos personagens. Um dos aspectos fundamentais do estilo é o mikiri, elemento de fundo responsável por conectar e dar movimento à composição. Água, terra, ar e fogo são algumas das possibilidades utilizadas para construir esse cenário.

Desenhos de gatos realizado pelo Vinicius — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

A proposta é que o desenho não seja visto apenas como uma imagem isolada, mas como uma composição que acompanha o corpo. “Hoje eu vejo a tattoo tradicional japonesa como um processo de amadurecimento do meu trabalho, onde já não vejo a tattoo como uma peça isolada e sim algo que veste o corpo”, explica.

Para alcançar esse resultado, cada elemento precisa ser pensado com cuidado. Até mesmo as flores seguem regras relacionadas às estações do ano, uma característica da composição tradicional japonesa.

Outro desafio está no equilíbrio entre os desenhos principais e os elementos de fundo, sem sobrecarregar a pele. Segundo Vinicius, a composição precisa respeitar as características de cada corpo e manter a harmonia do conjunto.

O resultado também é pensado para causar impacto visual. O tatuador aposta em cores saturadas e contrastes fortes entre tons e linhas pretas, características que, segundo ele, ganham ainda mais destaque quando a tatuagem é observada pessoalmente.

“Na rua, o impacto visual é muito maior. As pessoas lama muito sobre a força que tem a tattoo que eu faço, cores saturadas e preto bem forte, é um contraste que chama muita atenção”, afirma.

Atendendo em Sorocaba há cerca de três anos, Vinicius ainda busca ampliar a divulgação de seu trabalho na cidade. Para ele, existe um público interessado em conhecer a estética japonesa, mas também é importante apresentar a riqueza cultural que envolve esse tipo de tatuagem.

O profissional ressalta que o estilo não deve ser associado exclusivamente à Yakuza, organização criminosa japonesa frequentemente relacionada à tatuagem na cultura popular.

“É arte, história, cultura e respeito. É um universo muito rico, que merece ser conhecido e compreendido para além daquilo que normalmente é mostrado”, defende.

Trabalhos autorais do Vinicius Maciel — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Apesar das diferenças entre os estilos, os dois tatuadores enxergam a tatuagem como uma forma de expressão que pode assumir diferentes significados.

Para Fernanda, uma tatuagem não precisa necessariamente representar uma grande história ou uma reflexão profunda. Pode ser uma memória engraçada, uma paixão peculiar ou simplesmente uma ideia absurda com a qual alguém se identifica.

“Mas também acho que uma tatuagem pode simplesmente ser bonita ou encantadora. Nem tudo precisa ser levado tão a sério, né!? A vida tem bastante seriedade por conta própria”, comenta.

Vinicius, por outro lado, enxerga o processo de tatuar como uma experiência que também envolve transformações pessoais. Para ele, a dor, o tempo e a dedicação necessários para concluir um trabalho podem representar as próprias batalhas enfrentadas por quem decide marcar a pele.

“A pessoa que começa uma tatuagem não é necessariamente a mesma que termina. Existe algo muito particular em se conhecer diante da dor e descobrir até onde somos capazes de ir”, reflete.

No fim, seja por meio de animais em situações surreais ou de composições inspiradas em uma tradição milenar, os trabalhos mostram que a tatuagem não precisa seguir uma única fórmula. Entre referências, vivências e imaginação, a pele também pode se transformar em espaço para experimentar, criar e contar histórias.

À direita, um trabalho da Fernanda e, à esquerda, um do Vinícius — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Fernanda Paiva atende no estúdio Numa, no centro de Sorocaba, e Vinicius Maciel também atende na região central da cidade, próximo à Praça Frei Baraúna. Os dois trabalham com horário marcado.

articles.title: After Akvan, another cyclonic circulation brewing in Bay: IMD
articles.summary: IMD says a new cyclonic circulation may form over the Andaman Sea and southeast Bay of Bengal around late November as Cyclone Akvan weakens over Odisha.
articles.body: BHUBANESWAR: Another cyclonic circulation is likely to develop over the Andaman Sea and southeast Bay of Bengal around Nov-end, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said on Saturday, even as the remnant of Cyclone ‘Akvan’ weakened into a low-pressure area over interior Odisha.This was also indicated in the IMD’s latest extended range forecast issued for two weeks, starting from Nov 19 till Dec 2.Mrutyunjay Mohapatra, IMD DG, said they have not issued any specific forecast regarding the exact location, intensity or trajectory of the possible system so far, except its mention in the extended range forecast.According to Mohapatra, four to five cyclones form in the Bay of Bengal from Oct to Dec. Three cyclones have already hit Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.The DG said the situation witnessed this year carries a lot of similarity with the strong El Niño year in 1987, and could be attributed to the El Niño factor.“It will be too early to predict more details about the possible system. People should keep a close watch on their upcoming bulletins,” he said.The IMD’s indication of the possible development of a fresh system has, however, raised concerns among people already hit hard by the recent cyclones.Meanwhile, under the influence of Cyclone Akvan, Bhograi in Balasore district received the state’s highest rainfall of 108 mm in the last 24 hours. articles.title: COP31: New draft deal aims to avert collapse of talks at climate summit
articles.summary: The UN COP31 meeting in Turkey enters a second day of overtime as countries struggle to reach an agreement.
articles.body:
Efforts to avert the collapse of talks at the UN COP31 summit have faced further delays on the second day of overtime, as countries struggle to reach a new global climate deal.

A new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday which the Turkey and Australia co-hosts hoped would bridge the divide between nations.

Although it still includes no specific reference to "transitioning away from fossil fuels" - an omission in the previous draft that sparked threats of walkouts - it does acknowledge a previous commitment made by countries to do just that three years ago.

Countries were expected to reconvene to decide whether to approve a new deal, but that meeting was delayed on Sunday morning.

The president of the talks, Turkey's Environment Minister Murat Kurum, told the BBC he was "hopeful" of a breakthrough as he entered the summit on Sunday.

"We will be happy soon enough," he said.

But that outlook was not shared by the EU, which the BBC understands considers the new text to be a backward step.

The EU and Pacific states had been arguing against the removal of fossil fuels from the draft text. The EU has not yet reacted to this latest draft.

The Africa Group is likely to be disappointed at this latest iteration as it includes no specific figure on money for adaptation and instead kicks that decision to future meetings.

The new draft also includes for the first time a recognition that the world is on track to miss the crucial goal of keeping temperatures below 1.5C of warming.

These talks are approaching the longest-running in the COP history.

If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended until next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.

Just hours before the new text was published, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK's chief negotiator, struck a more hopeful tone, saying her team was still working to get an agreement.

A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.

The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday . On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.

As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.

COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday he believed concerns had been addressed.

"We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said. "We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues."

Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU were fighting to have a commitment to move away from fossil fuels put back into the final agreement, after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

Tuvalu's Climate Minister Maina Talia told reporters it was a "red line" for the low-lying Pacific nation: "We're talking about the root cause of all of this".

France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage (CCUS) - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.

"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.

In the latest text the commitments to CCUS have been reduced, which may be enough to alleviate the EU's concerns.

For the first time at a COP, the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal set under the Paris climate accord of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.

The world is entering a period called "overshoot".

Beyond this point scientists warn millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.

But Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.

He argued the summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.

One of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money - appears unresolved in the latest draft agreement.

Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - a figure that was then removed.

"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.

Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.

"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

articles.title: Epstein’s Russia obsession: 17 Young women, oligarchs and a desperate bid for redemption
articles.summary: Convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein continued recruiting women from Russia and other former Soviet states while cultivating ties with wealthy
articles.body: Convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein continued recruiting women from Russia and other former Soviet states while cultivating ties with wealthy businessmen and senior officials in the country, seeking to restore his standing among the global elite after his 2008 conviction, an investigation has found. At least 17 women from Russia and other former Soviet countries were drawn into this sex-trafficking network.Based on interviews with more than two dozen people familiar with Epstein’s Russian connections and a review of hundreds of pages of documents, news agency Reuters found that Russia was both a source of women drawn into his sex-trafficking network and a potential route back into influential circles.Three of these 17 women, identified in the investigation, later sought justice for his abuse and exploitation.Epstein’s interest in Russia began with its modelling industry. In the years following the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, modelling scouts travelled across the region looking for young talent. French scout Jean-Luc Brunel, who worked with Epstein, recruited women from Eastern Europe and brought them to Paris and the United States, according to people interviewed by Reuters.Former model Thysia Huisman recalled meeting Epstein at a party hosted by Brunel in Paris in September 1991. She said a Russian girl who appeared to be in her early teens spent much of the evening on Epstein’s lap.“The girl said modeling work was not good, but ‘Jeffrey takes care of me,’” Huisman told Reuters. “It was creepy,” she added, recalling the girl’s apparent age. Reuters said it could not independently confirm the party or the identity and age of the girl.Epstein made two known visits to Russia, in 1998 and 2002. The first took him to Sarov, a closed city associated with the Soviet Union’s nuclear weapons programme. His second trip included Moscow and St Petersburg, where he travelled with Brunel and Ghislaine Maxwell, according to flight records and people familiar with the journey.After pleading guilty in Florida in 2008 to prostitution-related charges, including soliciting an underage girl, and serving 13 months in jail, Epstein increasingly sought to cultivate Russian elites, the agency found.His contacts included Russian real-estate tycoon Vladislav Doronin and former deputy economy minister Sergey Belyakov. Emails reviewed by Reuters showed Epstein sought to use Belyakov as a channel to senior Russian leaders.In an April 2015 email to former Israeli prime minister Ehud Barak, Epstein wrote, “I suggest you send (Belyakov) a note,” saying Russian president Vladimir Putin and his advisers “would benefit from spending some time with Jeffrey to discuss markets, currency and the financial system”.Reuters found no evidence that Epstein ever met Putin, worked for Russian intelligence or acted on behalf of the Russian government. An apparent effort to arrange a 2011 meeting with Putin was ultimately abandoned, with people familiar with the episode describing the proposed appointment as “a charade”.Epstein’s Russian connections also extended through modelling agencies. Reuters reported that Brunel’s Miami agency, MC2 Models Management, recruited heavily in Russia, while Epstein provided accommodation for some models. One former model, Svetlana Pozhidaeva, told Reuters that Epstein sexually abused her and used financial and immigration arrangements to make her dependent on him.Epstein died in a Manhattan jail in 2019 while facing federal sex-trafficking charges involving minors. However, the report said that efforts to gain influence in Russia produced no major business deals or demonstrable access to Putin. articles.title: Three dead, 36 missing after fire tears through Indonesia confectionery factory
articles.summary: A fire tore through a candy factory in Indonesia’s Banten province on Saturday, killing three people and leaving 36 workers unaccounted for as rescue
articles.body: A fire tore through a candy factory in Indonesia’s Banten province on Saturday, killing three people and leaving 36 workers unaccounted for as rescue teams searched the damaged building. Fifteen people were rescued alive, including four who sustained injuries.The blaze broke out at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in Serang district, which borders Jakarta. The facility manufactures Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snacks.The National Search and Rescue Agency said rescue teams were continuing to search for the 36 missing workers, while firefighters battled flames and carried out cooling operations more than 12 hours after the fire began.“The fire is still burning in several locations, and firefighting teams are continuing extinguishing and cooling operations,” said Rizky Dwianto, an operations official at the Banten Search and Rescue Agency.Firefighters from Serang district and Banten province were tackling fires in several sections of the facility, Dwianto said. Rescue personnel were searching different parts of the factory for workers who might be trapped, with local firefighters and the Indonesian Red Cross assisting the operation.Television footage showed flames engulfing the three-storey factory and thick black smoke billowing into the sky. Images from the aftermath showed twisted metal, charred roofing and debris scattered across the floor of the damaged building.Outside the factory, anxious relatives gathered as they waited for news of family members they had been unable to contact.The cause of the fire was not immediately known. Authorities had not established whether all 36 missing workers were inside the factory when the blaze broke out. articles.title: Strictly Come Dancing noise disruption prompts BBC apology
articles.summary: Lancashire police says a mobile phone has been seized and it is assessing whether any criminal offences may have taken place.
articles.body:
The BBC has apologised "for any offence caused" after lewd audio was heard during the live broadcast of Strictly Come Dancing.

A recording of sex noises appeared to be playing from the audience in Blackpool's Tower Ballroom as judge Motsi Mabuse gave feedback early in Saturday's episode. She paused before joking: "It's not me."

At the end of the programme, presenter Emma Willis apologised to viewers "if you heard any audio disruptions". A BBC spokesperson also issued an apology and said it was "investigating how this happened".

Lancashire police said it was assessing whether any criminal offences may have taken place, after receiving a formal complaint and a mobile phone being seized.

The moment was streamed on social media by content creator Daniel Jarvis, whose videos include pranks. He appeared to place a phone call before the audio began playing in the ballroom, and suggested he was trying to target judge Craig Revel Horwood for his "bullying".

Jarvis has previously claimed he was responsible for sex noises disrupting Match of the Day in 2023 .

Willis told viewers: "Before we see the judges' leaderboard, we'd like to apologise if you heard any audio disruptions earlier in tonight's show and for any offence caused."

A BBC spokesperson said in a statement: "We apologise to any viewers offended during the live broadcast of Strictly this evening.

"We are investigating how this happened."

An edit will be made to the programme available on BBC iPlayer.

articles.summary: The town of Tupancireta in Brazil's southern state of Rio Grande do Sul was assessing the damage on Saturday after a powerful storm killed at least three
articles.body: The town of Tupancireta in Brazil's southern state of Rio Grande do Sul was assessing the damage on Saturday after a powerful storm killed at least three people and damaged thousands of buildings.Heavy rainfall and winds reaching speeds of 114 kilometres per hour (71 mph) struck the town early Friday, according to Brazil's National Meteorological Institute (Inmet). The state Civil Defence agency said the extreme weather was caused by a supercell, a rare and powerful thunderstorm characterised by a rotating updraft.Shop owner Marilia Amaral Ferreira described the devastation, saying she saw widespread destruction after stepping outside. She said buildings were damaged and residents were desperately calling for help, according to news agency Reuters.Thousands of homes damagedDrone footage showed the extent of the destruction, with damaged structures, twisted metal beams and roof tiles torn from a church.According to the civil defence agency, at least 5,000 homes were damaged. State Vice Governor Gabriel Souza said authorities were also investigating a possible fourth death.Felipe Rodrigues Lima, 35, his partner and two stepchildren lost their home in the storm. He described the experience as heartbreaking, saying the family would have to rebuild their lives from scratch.Meanwhile, firefighters worked early Saturday to provide food and water to animals trapped inside the municipal shelter after the storm.Firefighter Luciano Corje said the rescue operation was unusual as emergency teams were helping animals rather than people, adding that saving their lives was equally important.You use AI every day. articles.title: Miniature camera, exam fraud and public fury: South Korea education chief resigns after cheating scandal
articles.summary: South Korea’s education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned on Sunday, taking responsibility for failures in preventing cheating involving artificial
articles.body: South Korea’s education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned on Sunday, taking responsibility for failures in preventing cheating involving artificial intelligence (AI) ahead of the country’s highly competitive college entrance examination, after a separate exam scandal triggered public outrage and raised concerns over test security.President Lee Jae Myung accepted Choi’s resignation, the presidential office said, following criticism of the minister’s handling of the controversy surrounding the national tax accountant examination and preparations for the crucial Suneung college entrance test.The scandal erupted last Sunday when the top scorer in a national tax accountant examination confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to secure a near-perfect score. The disclosure came just four days before the Suneung, an annual nine-hour examination widely regarded as a gateway to prestigious universities and better employment prospects.In a statement posted on X, Choi acknowledged shortcomings in the government’s preparations and said he was stepping down.“The exam concluded without any major incidents... However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance,” he wrote.“Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation,” he added.Choi had faced criticism earlier in the week over remarks made during a parliamentary hearing on Monday. Asked whether he was confident that authorities could catch people attempting to cheat during the entrance examination, the 72-year-old replied: “Due to my age, I am not confident I could.”His response drew swift public backlash, with questions mounting over the government's ability to prevent technology-assisted cheating.Officials subsequently introduced a series of safeguards before Thursday’s Suneung. These included blocking public Wi-Fi in examination areas and placing stickers over clothing buttons to prevent the concealment of miniature cameras or electronic devices.Choi did not attend press conferences in the days leading up to the examination, with a vice minister instead announcing the preventive measures.Despite the additional precautions, officials identified 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices during Thursday’s examination. articles.title: AI is being used to clone real people's videos
articles.summary: Musicians, comedians and dancers are among those finding their videos cloned with AI generated characters.
articles.body:
Is this real or AI? It is a question increasingly asked underneath social media videos, and often difficult to tell.

But there is a new trend when it comes to digital manipulation. Across social media, AI-generated characters are appearing in videos that look remarkably similar to those posted by real people.

From musicians to dancers and comedians, content creators are finding their performances cloned by these characters that are designed to look funny, realistic, or hypersexualised.

Experts call the practice "reskinning" and say it is made possible by cheap, easy-to-use AI tools. People can discover their work has been copied by seeing a video of a character making the same joke or doing the same dance, even with the same background. Sometimes the AI version has millions more views than the original.

Some of the accounts identified by BBC Verify appear to be using these AI-generated videos to get views and likes, and to eventually make money. Others appear to be experimenting with AI to make people laugh or simply for the attention that comes with going viral. But the practice has angered content creators who say their original work is being stolen.

"A lot [of these accounts] are getting thousands of views, thousands of followers, just for literally doing nothing and stealing the stuff that we've created," says Sophie Lloyd, a UK-based guitarist who tours with US rapper Machine Gun Kelly, who has spent years building a successful online presence.

Lloyd says videos of her performances have been repeatedly reskinned by accounts that replaced her with over-sexualised AI-generated characters. One Facebook account published hundreds of short videos of a guitarist called "Mila Vasari" that had each gained thousands of views. BBC Verify found that at least three copied Lloyd's performances and used the exact same music, movements, and even facial expressions.

BBC Verify did not find any evidence that "Mila Vasari" is a real person. The videos on the Vasari account also contain visual inconsistencies that suggest AI was used to create them, including distorted fingers playing chords that don't match the music, and guitar strings that fail to move when strummed.

The account, which appears to be run from Canada, did not respond to questions about the purpose of these videos. Its profile links to a page devoted to Vasari on Fanvue, a subscription platform that allows creators to charge for content, including adult material. BBC Verify has found two other accounts fronted by AI-generated guitarists that have reskinned Lloyd's performances and use those avatars to sell and promote adult content.

But Lloyd is far from alone in having her content manipulated by AI.

"I've got so many messages from other artists and creators that have had the same thing happening to them," says Kjetil Krogstad, a Norwegian content creator known for videos showing him happily dancing in a suit while carrying a cup of tea.

In March, his followers alerted him to the fact that one of his videos had been reskinned using an AI-generated bunny. The post went on to attract millions of views - outperforming Krogstad's original video - before being deleted. When Krogstad looked into the account behind the bunny video, he found it promoting courses on how to make money from AI-generated content.

Dr Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, says that while these videos are sometimes made for fun, often the people behind the accounts copy videos that have already proven popular in the hope of attracting audiences and making money.

"What these tools allow people to do is just automatically take a viral concept that's already existing and to reuse it through these reskinning tools," she says.

Kendall sees this as part of a wider online "hustle culture", in which accounts seek to turn users' attention and engagement into money - be it through subscriptions to fan pages featuring adult content, risky cryptocurrency products like meme coins, or monetisation features on social media platforms.

And making these copies "conventionally attractive, white, feminine" characters can help, Kendall says. "That's the kind of stuff that always floats to the top and is successful, it really conforms with these conventional cultural ideals of attractiveness, success, aspiration, beauty."

Dozens of people have taken to social media in recent weeks to call out the AI-generated accounts they found using their content without permission.

"I cannot explain how angry I am right now," Grace Roberts, a British car creator, said on Instagram. "Someone not only stole my video, but also changed me into basically the societal norm of what people want to watch, and this is literally my job," she said, showing the original video of herself wearing jeans, smiling and covering her ears at a drag car race next to an AI-generated version with a blonde woman in a short dress.

"I put the videos side by side and I could see it was my exact facial movements, how my body moved, the exact same background and even the people around me were completely copied," she told BBC Verify. "It was just me that had been altered."

"I pay for the cars, I build the cars, I pay for the cameras, the filming equipment, and then someone can just hit download on their computer, change it, and then make money off the back of my video," she added.

Her concerns are echoed by other content creators who fear these AI-generated accounts could cost them valuable exposure, followers, and potential income.

American comedian Julia Jasunas, who called out having her jokes stolen online by AI, said in a recent Instagram video: "The thing that is most concerning is these AI bots are going viral and people think that they're real people.

"And for context, comedians post their stand-up clips online to get you to come out and see live comedy," she said, adding that comedians spent a long time crafting jokes on stage and honing them into punchy lines.

Equity, the UK's largest entertainment union, has called for new laws to protect performers against the unauthorised use of their work by AI, arguing that existing copyright legislation is inadequate.

But legal protections are only part of the challenge. Identifying those responsible for copying the videos, and stopping them from doing it again, can also prove difficult.

Stopping these pirated performances is a game of whack-a-mole, says Alwyn Cruz, who has made a name for himself on social media by exposing AI musicians. "You don't even know who's making these [videos]. And then if you shut it down, they're just going to create another," he says.

"It's not only guitarists that are being cloned: there are drummers, taekwondo players that are being cloned, and I've seen this all over the internet."

Meta told BBC Verify it had a policy of alerting users when their videos were reposted without permission and was exploring ways to limit the reach of the accounts that repeatedly did this.

Earlier this week the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said the platform is also "working quickly on ways to catch copies that are harder to spot, like when someone takes scripts or jokes and uses AI to swap out the visuals".

But for artists like Lloyd, the damage may already be done. "It takes years to master an instrument and seconds to take and rip it off as something else - and then people don't even know it's you."

articles.title: EU deal: 'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen?
articles.summary: Theresa May, David Cameron and Tony Blair have weighed in on Burnham's plans on moving closer to the EU, but the prime minister's message itself is not very precise.
articles.body:
"Move on!" That's Theresa May's frank instruction to Andy Burnham.

She spent years wrangling with the EU to try to forge a decent Brexit deal before being shoved out of her job by her party. Her leadership was broken by Britain's relationship with Brussels. Now she is warning the current resident of No 10 not to risk the same.

In a rare interview, Baroness May - who presided over negotiations with the EU between 2016 and 2019 - told me Burnham ought to respect the public's decision 10 years ago, not "pat them on their head" as if they gave the wrong answer and should have "another go".

And she said she was "aghast" at what he was doing, dangling the possibility of rejoining the EU, warning it would absorb huge amounts of government effort.

"The hours that have to be put in, it's across the whole of government," she said. "It's not just prime ministerial time, [it's] cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations."

But while some on his own side are very keen to get on with a campaign to rejoin the EU - and the foreign secretary tells me this option is on the table - May is not the only voice urging caution.

Earlier this month David Cameron also said starting a conversation about rejoining would be "long and painful".

And former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair has told the Sunday Times this weekend that Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology .

Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'

The prime minister's precise message on Europe is, maybe characteristically, not that precise.

From the by-election platform in the summer where he promised not to reopen old arguments and emphasised he was not proposing the UK considers rejoining, to telling the BBC the country could "go all the way" and go back in, to now the promises of a "national conversation" and "brainstorm" with the EU - his words have varied over time.

No 10 plainly wants to move closer to the EU, even if ministers suggest there really is no end fixed position and so this period of working it out is genuine.

They tell me that, in private, "Andy is pretty clearly where he is publicly - he does think it's a big discussion we have to have as a country, it's a national discussion in the context of the 10 year plan, but also has to involve the Europeans".

In other words, even though he makes no secret that he'd like to be in the EU and wishes we had never left, the prime minister won't conclude whether he'll promise to take the country back in until he has a better idea of what relationship he might get out of the EU - and, perhaps too, how the public responds.

Two quick reminders: Burnham has said it wouldn't happen before another election; and, remember there are elections in Europe too. This whole conversation might be transformed if Marine Le Pen becomes the president of France, or the march of other parties who are suspicious of Brussels continues.

The prime minister's body language in Brussels yesterday, though, and his proclamation that it was a "good day" for Britain, displays happiness in government at what they have achieved so far - closer ties on food exports, energy, and allowing young people to live and work more freely on both sides of the Channel.

Despite a last minute classic spanner in the works with a lack of agreement on tuition fees, the UK side feels positive they didn't back down on that issue yesterday, and the broader deals were concluded anyway.

And despite the protestations from the foreign secretary that the deals will all come into force whatever happens on fees, the government will start the legal processes to turn the agreements into law - although there are still plenty of opportunities for other countries to try and unpick them further down the track.

Of course, politicians' reactions to the deal depend which side they were on in the Brexit debate.

The Lib Dems, SNP, Greens and Plaid Cymru plead the case that it's not far enough. The Conservatives complain it's not fair, for example, that British farmers will have to follow EU rules to make life easier for those who trade with the bloc. Reform scream it's a betrayal of the 2016 vote.

But the feeling in government is the summit was a success and showed the EU will allow the UK to pick and choose where to cooperate, and is willing to listen to what the prime minister wants to do next. It's worth saying just as in any negotiation, the EU might always be up for giving if it receives in return.

Yet as May warns, doing deals with the European Union is simply, a long hard slog.

And one senior Whitehall source cautions the prime minister not to kid himself that an early feel-good factor doesn't mean future haggling would be a doddle: "British prime ministers can be oddly delusional about the EU - they can get seduced by the hope that good relationships with individual leaders will overcome the ideological inertia in Brussels which is overseen by French and German lawyerly high priests and priestesses.

"European leaders might actually be your friends, but they are not the ones in charge of decision-making in Brussels."

And a former negotiator warns that in his "brainstorm," the prime minister might well find the deal he's concluded this week just about rubs up against the limits of what can be done without going for the full-fat option - telling me: "There isn't much more to go with a strategy of incrementally building on the deal before it becomes quite a binary choice."

They add a reality check for any deal-making with the EU: "The EU have a very set way of doing things, that is more about their own unity than about who they are negotiating with."

Then of course, there is the politics at home. When cornered on this subject the prime minister and his cabinet often say the "British people will be the boss" - going on to cite polling that clearly displays disappointment with Brexit and a discernible interest in going back in.

But that's not the same as polling suggesting the public is demanding the government puts it at the top of the list.

As one senior Labour figure puts it, there has "certainly been a shift - and an openness to have the conversation" about rejoining, but the PM "has to be really careful about locking himself into a manifesto commitment that alienates a lot of people" alongside plenty of voters who might welcome a move.

What of May's warnings about getting tangled up in EU talks at the exclusion of all else?

One government insider from the time asks: "Can you even remember anything else that happened between 2017 and 2020? It's extremely naïve to think he can do all the other things that are extremely pressing, like defence, or Neets, while trying to play out a future with the EU - it won't happen."

It's worth noting, as some ministers do privately, that Burnham himself was not working in Westminster during the most intense struggles over leaving the EU - an advantage perhaps, that he doesn't carry that baggage, or a gap in his experience of how bad it was.

And yet, the prime minister - who, crucially, is confident in his ability to communicate with the public - is plainly resolved on exploring going back into the European Union, and choosing to take that argument on.

After what the government considers to have been a successful summit, that adventure looks more tempting to the many in Labour's tribe who think he is right to do exactly that.

After the last 72 hours, opportunity is knocking - but the warnings from prime ministers past ring out too.

Under May, Brexit affected nearly everyone and everything - trying to go back in under Burnham could perhaps affect everyone and everything too.

articles.title: Barnham vote 'sent powerful message', say politicians
articles.summary: MPs and councillors react to Barnham's symbolic vote to "leave UK" in protest at asylum seeker plan.
articles.body:
Local politicians have called on the government to take notice of a referendum held in the village of Barnham and re-think its plans for housing asylum seekers nearby.

Ninety-four percent of the 274 people who took part voted to become independent of the United Kingdom as a way of protesting against a proposal to house migrants at the former RAF Barnham military base.

The police and crime commissioner for Suffolk said the symbolic result "sends a powerful message" while the leader of Suffolk County Council warned "society starts to collapse when politicians stop listening".

The Home Office says it recognises the strength of feeling and insisted that it is listening carefully to the concerns being raised.

No-one was surprised by the outcome of the poll which saw 257 people vote for the village ''to become an independent self-governing Crown dependency'' and just 16 vote against the idea. One ballot was spoiled.

The result has no legal basis, but there were warnings from local politicians for ministers not to ignore the result.

"It sends a powerful message that it is a completely unsuitable site.

"I hope just for once that the government will actually listen to local people," said Tim Passmore the Conservative Police and Crime Commissioner for Suffolk.

"That is what Andy Burnham said he would do, now it's time for action."

Terry Jermy is the Labour MP for Thetford, which is just two miles away from the base.

He said: "The people of Barnham have done a really good job in raising awareness of the issue and demonstrating the strength of feeling against these plans.

"The message to the government is that this MoD site is not suitable."

While Michael Hadwen, the Reform UK leader of Suffolk County council, said: "This is a clear demonstration of democracy at work.

"Barnham has said loud and clear that that the government cannot impose this base upon them and the government should start to listen because when things like this start to get ignored that's when society starts to collapse."

The estimated turnout of around 70% was lower than campaigners had been hoping for.

When a similar referendum was held in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington 89% of locals took part.

The chair of the residents association in Barnham said some people had decided not to vote after seeing the government ignore the result in Piddington and give planning permission for a nearby military base to be used for asylum seekers.

A Home Office spokesman said: "We recognise the strength of feeling in local communities and are listening carefully to the concerns being raised.

"The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1 billion saved in costs since the election.

"This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites.

"These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to reduce the impact on local communities."

The Home Office also pointed out that whilst it has submitted an application to obtain planning permission to use the Barnham site, it is still assessing the base and no final decisions have been taken on the site's future use.

Barnham's Labour MP Peter Prinsley, is due to meet the immigration minister later this week where he says he will draw her attention to the referendum result and express his continued belief that the site is too remote to house asylum seekers.

"I'm still optimistic the eventual outcome will be that this is not a suitable place," he said.

Earlier this month, the government awarded a £3.4m contract to the construction company Kier to assess the viability of the Barnham site and draw up plans for it to accommodate asylum seekers while their applications are processed.

Some campaigners believe that the firm will conclude that the site is inappropriate.

They have suggested that the accommodation blocks could need major renovation and that the sewage and water system may be in need of repair.

They also wonder if the ground around the former nuclear weapons base could be contaminated. No one seems to know the answer to these questions at the moment.

After the referendum result a picture of a Stone-curlew was unveiled as the new image on the village flag. The protected species has been sighted in the area and may present another obstacle to the site being used.

There could also be delays in accessing the site should the government decide to use it.

Suffolk Police has a lease to use the base for training and storage which requires the MoD to give six months notice if it wants to take it back.

Suffolk County Council has also vowed to continue its fight.

"If the government keeps ignoring us we will look for other means to stop this from happening," Hadwen said.

"And if the government does decide to go ahead I will look at all legal means to stop those gates from being opened."

There seems to be a lot of obstacles to overcome and the referendum result appears to have given campaigners added impetus.

articles.title: ‘I have no son, I should ensure my daughter isn't burdened with these responsibilities’: At 80, Uttar Pradesh Baljor Singh organised his own ‘Tehrvi’ to spare his only daughter the burden of post-death rituals
articles.summary: Now this is an unusual story but also heartfelt and thought provoking.
articles.body: Now this is an unusual story but also heartfelt and thought provoking. An 80-year-old man in Uttar Pradesh’s Baghpat district made headlines after he organised his own ‘Tehrvi’ ceremony for an extremely personal reason. Baljor Singh organised a huge ‘daawat’ and called all his relatives (rather big fam jam) and decided to do his own post-death rituals so that his only daughter would be free of a huge responsibility. For those who don’t know, ‘tehrvi’ is a traditional post-death Hindu ceremony.Now it wasn’t an ordinary gathering. But what would ordinarily be a solemn gathering following someone's death became an occasion where Singh himself welcomed friends and relatives. He organised and shared a meal with over 900 people.The significance of TehrviTehrvi, also known as Terahvin or Terahvi, is a Hindu death-related ceremony traditionally observed on the 13th day after a person's death. It is one of the most crucial occasions for family members who come together and perform religious rituals along with offering prayers for the departed soul.The unusual gatheringThe unusual event took place in Johri village in the Baraut region of Baghpat, Uttar Pradesh on November 15, 2026. Singh was concerned about his only child Pinky. He wanted to make sure that she would not have to be buried under the financial and social responsibilities associated with organising his post-death rituals after he was long gone.His unusual gesture also gave him an opportunity to meet friends, relatives and villagers. The incident was reported on social media and The Times of India.Why did Baljor Singh organise his own Tehrvi?For Singh, it was a hard but important decision. The unconventional gathering was meaningful and also for his daughter. It was about taking responsibility for something he believed could otherwise become an additional burden for his daughter. So he decided to complete the rituals himself while he was alive.As per NDTV reports, he said, "The thought occurred to me that since I have no son, I should ensure my daughter isn't burdened with these responsibilities. I am performing this task while I am still alive."Singh has one daughter, Pinky, who is married with kids. His family includes his son-in-law, Sukhpal, three granddaughters and a grandson, Mukul. Singh also said that he owned two bighas of agricultural land, which he had already given to his grandson.A Tehrvi with 900 peopleAs per media reports, eight cooks were hired to prepare food for approximately 900 guests. The menu included puris (fried Indian bread), vegetable curry and sweets. A traditional havan was also conducted as part of the ceremony.Relatives, villagers and people from neighbouring areas attended the gathering. Uttar Pradesh minister KP Singh was also present and congratulated Baljor Singh on his unusual initiative.Passing on the family responsibility to his grandsonAnother important part of the gathering was the traditional pagdi ceremony, which symbolises the transfer of family responsibilities following the death of a family's patriarch in certain North Indian communities.Instead of waiting for the customary occasion, Singh performed the ritual himself. He tied his turban on the head of his grandson, Mukul, symbolically passing on the responsibility of looking after the family to the next generation.Speaking to NDTV, Pinky, the daughter said, "It feels good", describing her feelings about the unusual arrangement. She added that they hoped he would continue to enjoy good health and guide them as the family elder.His story is a reminder that sometimes a parent's concern for a child's future extends beyond providing financial security. articles.title: 6 buyers won back their pre-construction apartment deposits after a developer moved completion forward by a year but notified them six months later; Supreme Court of British Columbia ruled the delay breached disclosure rules
articles.summary: In a 2025 ruling, six pre-sale apartment buyers in British Columbia won the right to cancel their purchases and recover their deposits after a developer
articles.body: In a 2025 ruling, six pre-sale apartment buyers in British Columbia won the right to cancel their purchases and recover their deposits after a developer moved their completion date forward by a year and did not deliver the notice for six months. The six had signed contracts in 2022 for strata units in a multi-phased development in Langley, and the Supreme Court of British Columbia ruled that the delay breached the province’s disclosure rules. The developer had responded to the buyers’ refusal to close by issuing notices to complete and alleging default, but the court sided with the six purchasers.A completion window moved up a year in February 2024, yet buyers were told only in AugustAccording to Allen / McMillan Litigation Counsel (AMLC), the six purchasers signed contracts in March 2022 to buy pre-sale strata units in the development. On 29 February 2024, the developer filed an amendment with the Superintendent changing the estimated completion window from October to December 2025 to October to December 2024. The purchasers did not receive the amendment until 28 August 2024, just over a month before the new window began, which left them little time to prepare for early possession, strata fees and carrying costs. They started a court action in October 2024, and the Supreme Court of British Columbia decided the case in 2025.What the Supreme Court of British Columbia ruling decided, why a one-year earlier completion date was a material factIn the case known as Ye v. Vesta Properties (Latimer) Ltd., decided in 2025, the court held that the developer breached section 16 of the Real Estate Development Marketing Act by not giving timely notice of the one-year acceleration. It treated the change as a material fact because it directly affected the purchasers’ financial planning, including their ability to prepare for strata fees, mortgage obligations and other carrying costs. Citing an earlier British Columbia case, the court confirmed that significant changes to completion timelines may justify cancelling a contract. The developer had filed the amendment with the Superintendent within 30 days, but the purchasers did not receive it during the whole intervening period, and in that time they reasonably understood that completion would not happen until October 2025.How a short-notice completion date deepened the harm, and the two findings that let buyers cancelWhen the developer later imposed a completion date on short notice, the court found that this did not ease the prejudice caused by the late notice but made it worse. AMLC reported in its March 2026 summary of the decision that the court reached two conclusions. First, the one-year acceleration made the original disclosure statement materially false or misleading, which required the developer to file an amendment under section 16(1)(a)(ii) of the Act. Second, the developer’s failure to give purchasers the amendment within a reasonable time, in breach of section 16(1)(b), entitled them to rescind, meaning cancel, their contracts under section 23(1) and to recover their deposits.What the Real Estate Development Marketing Act requires developers to disclose to buyersThe British Columbia Financial Services Authority explains that purchasers of development units in the province are protected by the Act, and that a developer who has breached it cannot enforce a purchase agreement against a purchaser. Developers file disclosure statements describing the material facts about a development, and if any of those facts are omitted, changed or misrepresented, they must also file an amendment. Purchasers are entitled to a copy of the filed statement, and of any filed amendment, before they enter an agreement for sale or lease, although fees apply for retrieving copies. The authority does not enforce purchasers’ rights, which are governed by contract law, but it can investigate complaints and take regulatory action against developers.Situations in which pre-sale buyers can cancel, from a seven-day window to unmet conditionsThe British Columbia Financial Services Authority lists several circumstances in which a purchaser may cancel. A purchaser has seven days after signing to cancel by serving written notice on the developer. A purchaser may also cancel if they are entitled to a disclosure statement but do not receive one, or if the statement contains a misrepresentation or an omission. If satisfactory financing commitments or building permits have not been obtained nine months after the initial disclosure statement was filed, and no amendment arrives within 12 months of that filing, a purchaser may cancel at any time after the 12 months until the required amendment is received.What buyers recover after cancelling and the pre-sale risks that remain, from delays to price dropsAll deposits a purchaser has paid, including any interest earned, must be returned promptly on cancellation of a purchase agreement. Purchasers can also bring a civil claim against a developer and its directors for any misrepresentation, and under contract law they may ask a court to order compensation for a breach. Pre-sale units are bought before construction starts or finishes, and the authority lists three risks: delays that lead to an extension or termination of the contract, a price rise that increases the cost, and a price fall that reduces the value. Buyers may assign a pre-sale contract to someone else if it allows, but the same risks pass to the new buyer, and an assignment fee paid to the developer, plus any extra cost paid to the seller, may not be recoverable if the contract is not completed. The authority advises reading the disclosure statement carefully and getting advice from a lawyer or licensed real estate broker before signing an assignment.You use AI every day. articles.title: Daphne du Maurier's grandson delves into his family's history
articles.summary: Photos showing the author and her family have been shared for the first time by her grandson.
articles.body:
A set of photos of globally renowned 20th century author Daphne du Maurier has been shared by her family for the first time.

The photos show du Maurier in a series of family images, in settings including around Cornwall where she lived and did most of her writing - she died in 1989.

Her eldest grandson Paul de Zulueta found the pictures while researching a new book telling the personal story of his grandmother's artistic dynasty.

He said: "They were all tucked away in my mother's box. She said you might find this amusing - there's a box of photos here."

Du Maurier's novels which include Rebecca, Frenchman's Creek and Jamaica Inn continue to enthral readers, and often make the dark and brooding Cornish landscape central to the story.

Rebecca, written in 1938, has sold about 30 million copies worldwide and several of her novels have been made into TV shows and films.

Her grandson says writing about his ancestors and his famous grandmother has helped him understand her better.

De Zulueta was given access to du Maurier's private letters and photos, kept by his mother and his aunt.

His book Last Night I Dreamt tells of her connection to Ferryside, on the banks of the river Fowey in Cornwall, which has been a du Maurier family home for 100 years.

She first stayed there when she was 19, and it is where she wrote her first novel, The Loving Spirit.

Bodinnick, near Fowey, is also where she met her husband, Lt Gen Sir Frederick Browning, affectionately known as Tommy within the family.

When asked to pick two of the photos, De Zulueta referred to one showing the couple walking arm in arm not long after they married, and another of them in a boat.

"This is a particularly nice photograph of Daphne and Tommy in Fowey. Tommy my grandfather was wearing his brown leather jerkin.

"And of course this one is taken just outside of Ferryside in 1932. It must have been around the time of their honeymoon more or less, as they got married in July1932.

"So that photograph is particularly special I think."

De Zueleta visited his grandmother in Fowey as a child every school holiday.

He remembers her being great fun, very mischievous and "someone with a great sense of humour, who filled a room with laughter", rather than the reclusive figure she is often described as.

He said: "She was extraordinarily happy here.

"And she said when she first came down to Cornwall 'this is the freedom that I have long sought.

"The freedom to write and the freedom to walk, the freedom to be by myself'."

She later moved to Menabilly, the house that was the inspiration for Manderley, the country estate in Rebecca.

Rediscovering his grandparents' relationship from the perspective of an adult has been a voyage of discovery for De Zulueta, who now believes his grandfather had Post Traumatic Stress Disorder after the war, for the rest of his life.

Browning's wartime service culminated in commanding airborne forces in the flawed Operation Market Garden, where thousands of troops parachuted into the Netherlands trying to seize key bridges from the Germans.

De Zulueta now recognises the stress his grandfather's absence would have had on the couple and the pressures of war meant "we need to judge the era softly".

He said: "They [Tommy and Daphne] had a very loving, deep relationship but it was unsettled at times.

"My grandmother was bisexual and she did also have an affair in 1942."

"I think Daphne regretted that affair, the family have never admitted to it, but I discovered a letter," he added.

Her grandson said reading her correspondence meant he had "got to like her a lot more".

"I always felt Daphne neglected him and therefore I was always in my grandfather's camp, but the more I read more about her life, I began to admire and respect her a great deal more.

"She was a great writer and how could she possibly be up in London trying to write books with my grandfather."

"She had to be in Cornwall because that was the ground-swell of her imagination," he added.

articles.title: Jersey minister open to grant for fourth Bergerac series
articles.summary: A Jersey minister gives his "in principle" approval for providing funding for a fourth season.
articles.body:
Jersey's government is "supportive" of awarding a grant towards filming the latest series of Bergerac.

Minister for Sustainable Development deputy Gerald Voisin said "in principle" he backed Visit Jersey and the government supporting a fourth series of the detective drama reboot.

The government has already given more than £700,000 in grants to the crime series which is due to resume filming in 2027, with £1.5m spent over series one and two.

Voisin said the grant would be "conditional" on factors including a set number of production trainee positions and verification of a minimum spend.

UKTV said about 2.4 million viewers tuned in to watch the premiere and Visit Jersey has used it as a marketing peg to attract visitors to follow in the footsteps of Jim Bergerac who is played by Damien Molony.

The tourism body's chief executive Tricia Warwick said it had "impactfully raised Jersey's profile as a visitor destination".

While parts of the series are filmed in Jersey, filming has also taken place in the UK.

Voisin said the government "made sure that exterior shots of Jersey feature prominently within Bergerac" but script and scene planning was "a matter for the production team".

The original series starring John Nettles as Bergerac ran from 1981 to 1991 with more than 15 million viewers tuning in to the first episode on BBC One.

A UKTV spokesperson responded to the minister's comments: "At this stage, there is no news to share in relation to a fourth series."
