articles.title: Man who studied drama in young offenders' institution now a West End actor
articles.summary: Joseph Langdon, who stars in the Bristol Old Vic's production of Cinderella, learned to act while detained.
articles.body:
A former young offender who became a West End actor says taking drama lessons while he was detained was the best decision he ever made.

Joseph Langdon, who grew up in south London, was convicted of gang-related crimes at the the age of 16. But while in a young offenders' institution, he was offered drama lessons through a scheme with the Bristol Old Vic.

Langdon said the lessons taught him "that I could make something of my life, and introduced me to this world I did not think was possible".

The actor, who will play the prince in the theatre's Christmas production of Cinderella: A Fairytale, said: "I count my blessings every day. I turn up to rehearsals with a huge smile on my face."

"I'm now working all over the world and have the most amazing life," he added.

"When I think of old friends from when I was a kid – some are dead now, some are in prison and I know that would be my life if it wasn't for Bristol Old Vic giving me a chance and hope."

Crane set to lift collapsed bridge out of harbour

Are digital memories helping us or holding us back?

'I focused on getting a baby, not what came next'

While in a young offenders' institution in Bristol, he was taught drama every week through a scheme run by the Bristol Old Vic Young Company.

"At first I was like, 'No I'm not going to go, I feel a bit too cool for this'.

"But when I did decide to go it was the best decision I ever made. I never skipped a lesson," he said.

At the end of his sentence, Langdon was told he could either move back to London and "get caught up in the same trouble" or move to Bristol "and start life afresh".

Langdon moved to Bristol, where he lived in youth hostels and halfway houses while training at the Old Vic through the Made in Bristol scheme - a free programme for young theatre makers.

He said coming out of prison was tough, but his support network kept him "on track".

The actor also worked at the theatre's box office and took part in various productions before returning to south London to study at Mountview drama school, thanks to a bursary scheme.

He said he was anxious about going back to the area he grew up in but "everybody was so supportive and proud".

After graduating, Langdon went on to act in numerous films and productions, including in the West End.

"Being adopted by Bristol has been the biggest blessing of my life," said Langdon, who returns to the city to star in Cinderella.

"The Bristol Old Vic has such a special, special, magical energy" and it is "truly an honour and a blessing to be part of that," said the actor.

Lucy Hunt, Bristol Old Vic's director of engagement, said Langdon understood "first-hand how a bit of belief in a young person can make a big impact on their lives".

"I am so happy he is back," said Hunt. "He is the best positive energy to have around and he's going to be amazing as the prince."

The Olivier Award-nominated adaptation of Cinderella was devised by Bristol artists Sally Cookson, Adam Peck and the Original Company and draws from various versions of the fairytale, including the Brothers Grimm story.

"Ultimately, it's a beautiful family show full of fun, magic and wonder," said Langdon.

Langdon now goes into schools and gives talks to "be that representation" for those interested in theatre.

He says he wants to "show other people from all different backgrounds, no matter who you are, that this is possible".

Cinderella: A Fairytale runs at the Bristol Old Vic from 27 November to 2 January.

articles.title: Near South Africa’s Orange River, researchers found two large mineral deposits beside a prehistoric skeleton’s spine; lab tests identified material commonly found in urinary stones
articles.summary: Discover how researchers found evidence of kidney stones in a prehistoric skeleton, revealing insights into ancient health problems linked to urinary conditions.
articles.body: Anyone who has had a kidney stone, or sat next to a friend who has, probably knows how much it can hurt. The problem is also much older than modern times. In a 1989 paper titled ‘A probable case of prehistoric kidney stone disease from the northern Cape Province, South Africa,’ Alan Morris and Allen Rodgers wrote about a skeleton found near South Africa's Orange River. Two large mineral deposits were found near its lower spine. Lab tests revealed what they were made of. The finding connected a person from the distant past to a health problem that many people still face today.The grave on the banks of the Orange River The skeleton came to light during excavations of isolated graves along the north side of the Orange River in the Cape Province of South Africa. The archaeologists discovered two calcium-rich deposits near the lumbar region, the lower portion of the spine. The skeleton belonged to an adult female who died at about 55 years of age. The paper's title called the case prehistoric. This finding provided insight into what could be a possible medical condition from ancient times. It also showed how much one grave could reveal about the daily health of people in the distant past.What the lab tests found It's difficult to identify hard lumps in a grave just by looking at them. So, the team ran some lab tests. They used X-ray powder diffraction and scanning electron microscopy. These methods help scientists find out what a material is made of. They both identified the deposits as apatite, a mineral form of calcium phosphate. Apatite is a common constituent of human urinary stones. These are hard lumps that can form in the kidneys and urinary tract. The deposits were not kidney-like in shape or in internal structure. But the authors provided an explanation. They suggested that the build-up on both sides of the body was caused by a long-running kidney problem. They called it a probable case, not a proven one.How scientists tell a stone from a pebble Another study explains why scientists cannot rely only on their eyes. Donatella Usai and colleagues discovered three stone-like objects in a grave at Al Khiday, Central Sudan, in 2013. In their 2017 paper published in PLOS ONE, the authors reported that one of the objects was found between the pelvic bones, and two other objects were found near the lower spine of an adult male. They were all about 26 to 30 millimetres in diameter. Ordinary rocks were ruled out because the objects were too light compared to rocks. They had a density of about 1 gram per cubic centimetre, while most rocks are 2 to 3. The minerals inside, hydroxylapatite and whitlockite, then suggested the prostate rather than the kidney or bladder.What the findings do and do not show These two cases are not the same. The Sudan stones were linked to a man's prostate. The South African findings pointed to a suspected kidney problem in a woman. However, both findings showed how scientists use minerals and location to work out what a lump is. The Sudan team argued that prostate stones can no longer be considered a purely modern disease. This matched the idea that people suffered from urinary stones for a long time. However, the limits still matter. Morris and Rodgers said that their case was probable, and the deposits did not match the shape of a kidney. The South African discovery did not prove that the woman died of kidney stones or even that she definitely had them. They only showed that a calcium-based material common in urinary stones was there close to her spine. Careful lab work turned a puzzling discovery into a small piece of someone's medical history, someone who walked the Earth a long time ago.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: The couple have been together for four years and were engaged in 2025.
articles.body:
Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.

Photos of the wedding on Saturday show the ceremony took place by a swimming pool with the pair standing under an arch covered in white flowers.

The singer's mother, Tish Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, were in attendance, Entertainment Tonight reported.

Grammy-winning Cyrus, who donned a white dress for the wedding, confirmed her engagement to the 28-year-old drummer during an interview with US TV show Good Morning America last year.

Miley Cyrus confirms engagement to musician Maxx Morando

She said Morando had got down on one knee for the proposal during a trip to Asia.

"I am not easy to surprise because I love to control every situation and I had completely surrendered and I'm telling you, I was so, so, so surprised," she said.

During an interview with Wonderland, Morando said he "had to be really sneaky" to keep his proposal plans a secret.

"We went to Tokyo first for a couple days, and then on to Kyoto. I think she had a sense that it was coming, so I was waiting until the very last moment of the very last day to throw her off the scent as much as I could," he said.

Cyrus, 33, had previously been married to Australian actor Liam Hemsworth but the couple separated in 2019.

The singer, whose hits include Flowers and Party in the U.S.A, married Hunger Games star Hemsworth in 2018 after the couple were in a relationship for a decade.

Speaking to British Vogue in 2023, Cyrus said she and 28-year-old Morando met after being "put on a blind date".

Morando is a drummer with LA-based band Liily. The band participated in NBC's Miley's New Year's Eve Party - hosted by Cyrus - in 2022, alongside musicians including Cyrus's late godmother Dolly Parton and David Byrne.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Telangana CM Revanth Reddy's remarks taking a swipe at critics within his own party have sparked a row amid growing signs of dissent in the state Congress.Addressing a public gathering in Siddipet on November 19, Reddy accused some party members of publicly highlighting the government's shortcomings while privately praising its work. articles.title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?
articles.summary: The number of Scots claiming disability benefits has risen sharply since the Covid pandemic - why?
articles.body:
Every month, more than 12,000 applications are made to Social Security Scotland for disability support.

The number of Scots receiving these benefits has risen sharply since the Covid pandemic, and is projected to hit one million by the end of the decade.

This has been driven in part by younger people and claims for mental health conditions.

The cost of the system has been growing, posing additional challenges for Scottish ministers facing a tight budget settlement.

But with the UK government considering a radical redesign of support in England and Wales, they insist that Scotland's welfare state does not need to be trimmed.

Why has there been such an increase in claims in Scotland, and can the government afford to continue its more generous approach?

Scotland has long had a higher rate of ill health among adults than other parts of the UK, often attributed to its history of heavy industry and relatively high levels of poverty in certain areas.

But the change seen in recent years has different roots.

There has been a notable uptick in disability across the UK since the Covid pandemic - and it is most pronounced north of the border.

The percentage of Scotland's working-age population, aged 16 to 64, reporting having a disability increased from 19% in 2020-21 to 28% in 2023-24 .

In children aged under 16, it doubled from 6% to 12%.

That has translated into a rising number of people receiving disability benefits - in total there are about 800,000 people in receipt of them today.

The Scottish Fiscal Commission says there has been a "shift in the age profile of applicants" since 2020.

Some 35% of the new applicants for Adult Disability Payment , since it was rolled out as Scotland's main disability benefit in 2022, have been people under 35. Over half are under 45.

Mental health is a key element in this, with 41% of the ADP caseload concerning "mental and behavioural disorders".

Almost half of those are "neurotic and stress related" conditions, such as anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder.

If you look back before social security was devolved to Holyrood, mental and behavioural disorders accounted for only 26% of the claims for Personal Independence Payments, the main disability payment in the UK system.

Among children, these conditions now account for 64% of applications in Scotland - with the number of people under 16 receiving the Child Disability Payment for them more than doubling from 30,000 in 2020 to 75,000 this year.

Meanwhile, mental health conditions play a much smaller role in benefit claims from older people, accounting for 13% of the Pension Age Disability Payment caseload - behind both back and joint issues and diseases of the circulatory system.

There are inevitably some who characterise it as the product of an overly sensitive "snowflake generation".

But others note that the current cohort of young people spent their formative years in lockdown before emerging into a cost-of-living crisis and the destabilising rise of AI - with polling suggesting that the majority believe they will be worse off than their parents .

Mental health charity Scottish Action for Mental Health (SAMH) says young people today are "growing up significantly more mentally distressed".

Chief executive Billy Watson said they face a "relentless" pace of life, with social media constantly exposing them to unsettling news and world events and unrealistic social comparison.

Data published this week from the Scottish Health Survey suggested that mental wellbeing - measured using an internationally-recognised scoring system - had recovered to pre-pandemic levels.

However, the 16 to 24 age group had the lowest score of any included, and around a quarter of young adults reported poor enough mental health to suggest a possible psychiatric disorder.

An independent review for the UK government by Prof Peter Fonagy last month said the problems faced by young people were real , with dramatically increasing cases of mental distress including depression and anxiety.

But Fonagy also warned of an "increasing risk of overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis".

He said this was because "diagnosis has become the primary gateway to support that could and should be available earlier".

This was echoed by Alan Milburn, author of the UK government's review of support for young people in England and Wales.

He said that "in too many places, diagnosis has inappropriately become the key that unlocks help", which has "created pressure on people to seek a diagnosis".

As an aside, it should be noted that while Milburn's review centred on employment prospects, benefit uptake does not always read across directly to this; Adult Disability Payment is not an "out of work" benefit like Jobseeker's Allowance.

The employment rate among disabled people in Scotland is more than 50%, and on the flip side studies have suggested that almost half of those not in education, employment or training are not claiming benefits either.

Milburn's review proposed sweeping changes to the youth support network in England and Wales, including faster access to mental health services and a complete replacement of Personal Independence Payments.

But in Scotland, "Pip" has already been replaced by Adult Disability Payment.

There was a very deliberate wave of publicity around the launch of the new benefit in 2022 - alongside the versions for children and pensioners - in a bid to increase uptake among people who might have been entitled to the likes of Pip, but never claimed.

With more money being spent on the Scottish system - it costs about £1bn a year over and above the block grant from Westminster - there is an easy narrative that it is inherently more generous.

A report last year concluded that it was more " significantly more compassionate " and "kinder in tone and approach".

However, it is worth noting that more than half of initial applications for ADP have been rejected, with 43% approved compared with 54% denied - broadly in line with the system in England and Wales.

There has been a steady increase in rejections since ADP was rolled out in 2022 - in the first few months only a quarter of applications were rejected, but over the past year it has been 67%.

Asked about this, Education Secretary Mairi McAllan said Social Security Scotland undertook a "very robust and close examination of all applications", and that people had to prove they were in need.

Last year also saw a record number of referrals rejected from NHS child mental health services , with ministers saying specialist services are only right for a small proportion of young people.

Even with an increase in rejections, the overall number of claims and the cost of the devolved social security system has been rising - and ADP alone makes up more than half of the total cost.

The last forecast from the SFC was for the social security bill to be £7.8bn in 2027-28 - within that, ADP accounts for £4.2bn, the pension-age disability payment £972m and child disability payment £659m.

By 2030-31, the cost is forecast to rise to £9.2bn - which has prompted questions from auditors and opposition parties alike about whether it is sustainable.

Ministers have repeatedly insisted that they view benefits as an investment in the people of Scotland.

But they have also said they will look carefully at Milburn's proposals.

A more generous system is not necessarily an easy choice, when it entails higher rates of income tax and cuts to other budgets.

There is also the possibility that changes down south could widen the existing £1bn funding gap, by cutting welfare spending at Westminster.

First Minister John Swinney has suggested that there are "potentially some significant financial implications that could be negative" for Holyrood.

But if money cut from benefits ends up being spent on education or local employment services - devolved issues - it would end up flowing back into the Scottish budget regardless.

Milburn's plan could apparently save about £200m a year by 2036-37, and while this would grow in subsequent years it should not represent a huge impact on devolved budgets.

And 10 years down the road the Scottish government's own public service reform plans, from the NHS to local councils, should have been worked through.

Who knows where we will be by then? The pace of change is relentless - in technology, in society, and in the health of the nation. The question is whether governments and policy can keep up.

articles.title: My son donated his body to science and became a 'silent teacher'
articles.summary: Barbara Scott's son has already donated his body to Edinburgh University's medical school to help students to learn about anatomy.
articles.body:
Fifteen years ago Barbara Scott signed documents to leave her body to medical science.

Her son Oliver McNeil Scott liked the idea and five years ago he also signed up to the body donation programme.

Barbara, from Lenzie in East Dunbartonshire, never thought her son would go before her - but in April 2025, Oliver died from colorectal cancer at the age of 48.

His body was signed over to the University of Edinburgh's medical school.

Despite not having a funeral for her son, Barbara has taken great comfort in his last act.

Known by those in the medical profession as silent teachers, every body donor contributes to the education of more than 1,000 anatomy students at the university every year.

Oliver, who was a regular marathon runner, had Ramsay Hunt syndrome, a rare neurological disorder caused by the same virus that results in chickenpox and shingles and affects facial nerves.

Barbara said being diagnosed with colorectal cancer only added to his determination to combat illness.

"He always wanted to do the best he could, and even during his illness, he researched all the new cures," Barbara said.

"In the end, he was going to be receiving a drug from America that he actually found himself, but unfortunately it was too late for Oliver.

"He knew how important research is and hopefully in 10 years his cancer will be very treatable, which was important for him."

Following Oliver's death, his body was taken from the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh to the University of Edinburgh's medical school.

Anatomy bequest co-ordinator Laura Shiels and her team of technicians work to ensure that every individual who gifts their body is cared for with dignity and respect.

"After Oliver died, it was really quite a shock to us," Barbara said.

"But when Laura took this on and explained to us all what was going to happen with Oliver, it was so nice."

Since Oliver's body arrived at the medical school in April 2025, Barbara has frequently visited the anatomy department so she can feel close to her son.

"It's just a lovely thing to sit here and think about him and about what a special thing he's done," she said.

"For Oliver, it is really life after death because he is facilitating students to find out more in the future about what's happened to him, how they can move forward. It's really, really important."

The University of Edinburgh is one of five universities in Scotland that receives body donations for medical education.

In the past five years there have been 200 people taken into their care at the end of life and there are currently 4,000 who have signed up.

The anatomy department can keep donated bodies for three years. Laura says they are vital in helping medical and biomedical students learn about the human body.

Tom Gillingwater, head of the department, believes body donors are possibly the most important people in the department.

"The only way that someone could properly have that experiential engagement with what lies inside the body, with what is the true anatomy of the body, is if they are able to look at, touch, and engage with a real body," he said.

"And when we want to do that looking underneath the skin, the only way we can do it is with someone who's willing to give us their body, where we can cut through that skin and look underneath it. These are our silent teachers."

The silent teachers also help practising surgeons, some from overseas, to pioneer new medical procedures.

Laura helps to care for donor families as they come to terms with loss and their relative's decision to leave their body to medical science.

John Green's parents, Alexandria and John, also donated their bodies to the university.

"The first time I heard about silent teachers was when my mother told me there were not going to be funerals because they were leaving their bodies to medical science," said John, from Sighthill in Edinburgh.

"I think at the time it never really registered."

After John's mum died from cancer in October 2024, he found the document she had signed to donate her body.

John said his parents had no connection to the university but he felt their decision may have been down to them wanting to spend their retirement money living, rather than saving for funerals.

After three years at the university, bodies are cremated in the Borders.

Every April, the anatomy department organises a memorial service for all the donor families, offering loved ones an opportunity to pay tribute and mourn.

About 500 relatives and medical students attend every year.

The names of the silent teachers who came into the university's care that year are read out.

John attended the service to honour his mum in April 2025.

"I was expecting to see maybe 30, 40 people and we'd sit and have a cup of tea and whatever," he said.

"To turn up and see how massive this was and how many people attended, it blows you away. I certainly did not expect something as big as that."

John's father died shortly before the service.

"I got the phone call to say that my dad was going to be delivered to the university on the same day as the service," he said.

Laura said: "We made a promise to this family that they would be together where possible in the departments that we have them together, and we'll cremate them on the same day."

John took great comfort from this but admitted he had struggled with his parents' decision.

"There is that part where there's no closure," he said.

"They've not gone yet, even though they're dead. I don't know how I'll be once I get that phone call from Laura to say 'they were cremated yesterday'."

Oliver's mum Barbara said his decision to donate his body was the best thing to happen to them both.

She said the memorial service was "amazing".

"For me personally it was much, much more emotional than having a funeral," she said.

"It was for all the other families, and they were going through the same thing. They made you feel that this gift was very special."

One of the important elements of the service is the line of photographs families have sent in of their loved ones.

"When you see them end of life and they've obviously been ill, it's actually so nice to see pictures being sent in when they are well and happy and with family," Laura said.

At the last memorial service, Laura put a photo of John Green's mum next to one of his dad John, who was being honoured this year.

John said: "When you walk up to the front and say 'right, where's my dad's picture?' and there's my mother beside him, you're like: 'Wow'.

"It then kind of hit home thinking 'this is the end', because I'm getting to say goodbye to both of them at the same time. That was like a closure in my mind."

In collaboration with the Scottish Chamber Orchestra, Scottish composer Jay Capperauld was commissioned to write a piece of music in tribute to the silent teachers.

He said: "It might be a three-year-long process before those families have been able to say a real and proper goodbye to their loved ones.

"I hope the legacy of this piece within the service of thanksgiving will be a moment of musical reflection and a real release of all of those emotions that may have been building up over those three years."

BBC Radio 3's Between the Ears , being broadcast at 19:00 on Sunday, follows Jay as he writes the Silent Teachers' piece, which will be played at every memorial service.

articles.title: Explained: 'Poverty, prejudice and profit', how Dhaka was repackaged as New Delhi
articles.summary: A narrow lane in Dhaka. Modest homes, roadside tea stalls, a canal and residents going about their daily lives.
articles.body: A narrow lane in Dhaka. Modest homes, roadside tea stalls, a canal and residents going about their daily lives. A woman points her camera at the surroundings and tells her online audience: “This is New Delhi.”The camera keeps moving. Tin-roofed houses are described as dirty and unhygienic. A neighbourhood in Bangladesh is presented as India's capital, while another livestreamer filming people drinking tea makes a grotesque claim about what is in their cups.These were not scenes from Delhi. They were filmed in Uttara and Tekpara, low-income neighbourhoods of Dhaka, by Chinese nationals.For months, the cameras reportedly kept returning to the same streets, homes and markets. Residents said they were filmed for hours, sometimes inside their own homes, without fully knowing where the footage was going or how their lives were being portrayed.Then, around November 7, the cameras began disappearing.The reports have since triggered an official response from New Delhi and increased surveillance by Bangladeshi law enforcement. But the most important questions remain unanswered: Who were these livestreamers working for? Why were Dhaka neighbourhoods being presented as Delhi? And was this a commercial content operation, an organised attempt to discredit India, or something more complicated?‘This is New Delhi’: What the livestreams showedIn its November 6 investigation, Bangladesh's Prothom Alo reported that Chinese nationals had been filming in Uttara's Sector 12 and the adjoining Tekpara area for months, often from morning until night. They were seen carrying two mobile phones, using one to livestream while apparently referring to material on the other.The newspaper said local residents estimated that more than 150 Chinese nationals were involved, although it acknowledged that no accurate count was available. Its reporters visited the neighbourhood on October 27 and November 3 and attempted to speak to 17 Chinese nationals. Most declined to answer questions.One livestreamer, identified as Mianmian and said to be from China's Sichuan province, was filmed beside a canal in Sector 12 on November 1. While showing the surrounding neighbourhood, she told viewers: “This is New Delhi. Their homes are extremely dirty. There isn't even a fan inside the tin-roofed houses. This place is quite underdeveloped, dirty and unhygienic, and the law-and-order situation is poor.”Another streamer, identified as Wang Wei, was reportedly filming at tea stalls in Tekpara when he told viewers: “Look, they are drinking tea. Do you know what kind of tea this is? This is cow urine tea. They drink cow urine tea.”Prothom Alo said it translated portions of the Chinese-language broadcasts using Google Translate and had the translations checked by four Bangladeshis familiar with Chinese.The issue extended beyond the misrepresentation of locations. Residents complained that cameras were repeatedly pointed at their homes and private lives, sometimes without permission.“Sometimes they enter our homes and start filming. We are not always properly dressed inside our houses. Imagine how it feels when someone suddenly walks into your home and starts recording,” resident Rozina Khatun told the Bangladeshi media outlet.Another resident, Papia Begum, said some streamers even entered bathrooms while filming. She said objections often led them to apologise and leave, but they returned later.A trail that predates the controversyThe November revelations were not the first reports of Chinese nationals filming in the area. A May 23 investigation reported that Chinese vloggers had been filming in Tekpara for hours at a time, sometimes using iPhones fitted with cooling fans.Videos from the neighbourhoods have also appeared on Chinese platforms such as Bilibili and Youku. Several reportedly carry titles using disparaging terms such as “poor”, “dirty” and “slum”, while focusing on low-income residents and their living conditions.In May, Bangladeshi media outlets reported on videos in which creators appeared to portray themselves as benefactors helping impoverished residents. One resident alleged that a vlogger had grabbed a young Bangladeshi man's collar in a video, apparently to “discipline” him.When disgust becomes currency: How viral outrage shapes perceptions of IndiaThe repeated circulation of videos portraying India through poverty, dirt and deprivation can also be understood through the idea of an epistemic project — the process through which selected images, labels and narratives shape how audiences understand a country. When viewers repeatedly encounter footage described as “dirty”, “backward” or “unliveable”, these portrayals can gradually become familiar reference points, influencing perceptions beyond the individual videos.Disgust, shock and anger can also make viewers stop scrolling, react to content and share it. Repeated exposure to such selective imagery can also reinforce stereotypes about an entire country.A March 2026 study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, involving five experiments and 1,051 participants, found that people tended to overestimate the emotional intensity of reactions in their social-media feeds. Such perceptions were associated with a greater willingness to share content.The commercial incentive is clear. JNU professor Srikanth Kondapalli told ANI that some Chinese creators seek online recognition and validation. “They want to establish a higher profile on Weibo, WeChat and other social networking platforms. Their social standing and prestige increase with the number of subscribers, likes and validation they receive for their videos,” he said.The commercial angle and unanswered questionsThere is also a commercial explanation offered by at least one person involved. When Prothom Alo approached a Chinese national identified as Fangyou, a local guide helped translate the questions. Fangyou said the livestreams on WeChat were part of product-promotion activities. He declined to explain why the group had selected that particular neighbourhood or why the broadcasts continued for such long hours.Ritu Akhter, a Bangladeshi woman who said she had worked as a guide for the Chinese nationals for several months, told the newspaper she earned between 700 and 800 taka a day. She said other local women were also doing similar work.Some shopkeepers were reportedly paid around 500 taka to allow filming in their pharmacies, where Indian consumer products such as shampoo, soap and Kesh King hair oil were used as backdrops for promotional livestreams.These accounts point to a possible commercial component, but leave key questions unanswered: which products were being promoted, who owned the accounts, who paid the creators and local facilitators, and why some broadcasts allegedly labelled Dhaka as Delhi. No publicly established evidence has identified a commissioning organisation or a funding trail.India objects; Bangladesh steps up surveillanceIndia's ministry of external affairs raised the matter on November 10. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, “We have seen media reports in this regard. Such efforts to present a distorted picture of any country are unfortunate.”Referring to reports of foreign elements being used to portray Dhaka as Delhi, he added: “Peddling of false narratives only undermines the credibility of those who are undertaking such actions and those who are behind them. And I would urge that authorities concerned must take action against such a report.”Bangladeshi authorities subsequently stepped up monitoring. Mohammad Khalid Mansur, officer-in-charge of Uttara West Police Station, told Prothom Alo that the activities of the Chinese nationals had declined after law enforcement intervention. Police and intelligence personnel were monitoring their movements, he said.According to the newspaper, some Chinese nationals were asked to produce their passports and visas and explain why they were undertaking the filming while visiting on tourist visas. They were also told to leave after their permitted stay expired.By November 11, the newspaper's correspondent had not seen Chinese nationals livestreaming in the areas visited. Resident Imam ul Islam, a rickshaw puller, said: “They would make videos here day and night. They filmed us and the passengers too. I haven't seen them for some time.”The China contrast: Censorship and ‘positive energy’The controversy also invites scrutiny of the information environment in which the footage was reportedly being circulated. China's domestic internet is not an unrestricted marketplace of images and opinions. Its authorities have established rules that direct platforms to regulate content and promote officially approved narratives.In September 2025, China's Cyberspace Administration (CAC) launched a campaign targeting posts it accused of exaggerating personal hardships, spreading pessimism and promoting “world-weariness”. Major platforms, including Weibo, Kuaishou and Xiaohongshu, were directed to remove such content. Critics viewed the measures as an attempt to curb narratives that could undermine the government's portrayal of economic progress.Freedom House's Freedom on the Net 2024 report also documented the removal of online content depicting poverty and economic hardship, including the censorship of the film Return to Dust and its title on Sina Weibo.This provides context for examining how narratives about poverty are regulated within China while some influencers have circulated disparaging portrayals of India. However, it does not establish that the Dhaka vloggers were acting on government instructions or had official backing.This record provides context for examining the contrast between the image of China promoted through its regulated digital environment and the freedom with which some creators appear to have circulated disparaging portrayals of another country. It does not, however, establish that the vloggers in Dhaka were acting under state instructions, or that Chinese authorities approved their broadcasts.A question of accountabilityFor Bangladesh, the immediate questions concern the rights of residents, the conduct of foreign visitors and whether filming or commercial activity breached visa conditions.For India, the issue is the circulation of content that allegedly attributes another country's locations and living conditions to its capital. For China, questions remain about the platforms carrying the broadcasts and whether their location claims and commentary were subject to any scrutiny.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'This is new India's response': BJP takes swipe at Pakistan over its minister's applause at Purana Qila
articles.summary: The BJP on Sunday took a swipe at Pakistan by sharing a video of Pakistan minister Musadik Malik applauding during the event at the Purana Qila.
articles.body: The BJP on Sunday took a swipe at Pakistan by sharing a video of Pakistan minister Musadik Malik applauding during the event at the Purana Qila. They shared the moment of Malik applauding at a presentation on Indian civilisation, Kashmir's culture and the Mahabharata and used it to get back at Pakistan's earlier remarks on Kashmir and India.BJP's national account shared a video montage of Pakistani leaders' statements on Kashmir featuring army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Musadik Malik. Their words are later juxtaposed with visuals of Malik and other delegates applauding at the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum.The video, edited with the track 'Ari Ari' from Dhurandhar as the background music, was posted by the BJP's national account. It juxtaposed clips of statements about Kashmir, India's water resources and Hindus.It highlighted the contrast between the remarks and the Pakistani minister's presence at an event showcasing India's cultural heritage."Those who lay claim to Kashmir, threaten to break up India and insult Hindus… were applauding India’s civilisation, Kashmir’s culture and the epic of the Mahabharata at the Purana Qila!" the BJP said in its post, adding, "This is the new India’s response!"The video carried captions highlighting remarks such as "Kashmir belongs to Pakistan", "We will cut hands of those who block our water" and "We are different from Hindus. Hindus are inferior". It then showed Malik and other attendees applauding during cultural presentations.The BJP also used captions to underline its political message. One read, "Those who claim Kashmir are applauding when Kashmiri culture is presented as Indian". Another said, "Those who threatened to cut India's hands were left clapping for India".The three-day SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum is being hosted by India at the historic Purana Qila. Malik, Pakistan's minister for climate change and environmental coordination, was among the delegates attending the event.During his address at the forum, Malik had invoked Mughal emperor Humayun and Sher Shah Suri, both associated with the construction of Purana Qila. articles.title: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia named biggest fossil fuel exporters of CO<sub>2</sub> as study traces global warming emissions from coal, oil and gas exports dating back to 1850
articles.summary: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia have been identified as the world's largest historical exporters of carbon dioxide emissions in a new analysis
articles.body: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia have been identified as the world's largest historical exporters of carbon dioxide emissions in a new analysis examining fossil fuel exports dating back to 1850. The findings shift attention from countries that burn coal, oil and gas to those that extract and sell them abroad. Published by climate news and analysis website Carbon Brief, the analysis estimates that Russia's exported fossil fuels generated almost 70 gigatonnes of CO2, followed by around 60 gigatonnes linked to Saudi Arabia and more than 25 gigatonnes from Australia. The results have renewed debate over which countries should bear responsibility for the damage caused by global warming.Why Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are being linked to historical global warmingMost assessments of a country's historical carbon emissions count the CO2 released within its borders. This means emissions are generally attributed to the country where fossil fuels are burned, rather than the nation that extracted and exported them. Carbon Brief's new analysis uses a different approach, known as extraction-based accounting, which assigns emissions to the country where the coal, oil or gas was produced, even if another country later used the fuel.According to Carbon Brief's analysis by Dr Simon Evans, the calculations cover fossil fuel exports from 1850 to 2025 and draw on data compiled by Robbie Andrew, a senior researcher at the Norwegian climate institute CICERO. The method estimates the CO2 that would be released when exported fossil fuels are burned. It therefore offers a different way to examine historical responsibility for global warming, rather than replacing conventional emissions accounting.The findings put Russia at the top of the historical fossil fuel export ranking, with almost 70 gigatonnes of CO2 attributed to fuels extracted there and burned overseas. Saudi Arabia follows with approximately 60 gigatonnes, while Australia ranks third with more than 25 gigatonnes. Venezuela is close behind Australia. Other major exporters identified in the analysis include Iran, Norway, the United Arab Emirates and Canada.Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia account for billions of tonnes of exported CO2Russia's position reflects its extensive coal, oil and gas resources and the volume of fossil fuels it has supplied to international markets. The analysis attributes an additional 69 billion tonnes of CO2 to Russia when emissions from its exported fuels are included. This places the country third in the overall historical emissions ranking under the extraction-based method, behind the United States and China.Saudi Arabia's position changes considerably when oil and gas exports are counted. The country becomes the world's fifth-largest contributor to historical warming under this accounting approach, with its cumulative emissions responsibility increasing more than fourfold. Australia also moves up the rankings, entering the top 10 historical emitters as its contribution more than doubles when emissions from exported fossil fuels are included.As The Guardian explains, the findings arrive as Australia co-presides over the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey. Fossil fuels account for about two-fifths of Australia's export economy, and the country has not set an end date for their use or export. Reports also state that Australian coal mines were still being approved with potential operating lives extending to 2088, raising questions about the gap between its climate diplomacy and continued fossil fuel production.The analysis does not suggest that these three countries are responsible for more historical warming overall than every other nation. The United States and China remain the two largest contributors under extraction-based accounting because both have burned substantial quantities of their own fossil fuels as well as importing energy from elsewhere. The distinction is that the new ranking isolates the emissions associated with exported fuels and highlights the role of major suppliers.How counting fossil fuel exports changes the ranking of historical pollutersThe shift in accounting also changes the position of countries that depend heavily on imported energy. Germany, India, France and Turkey fall in the rankings when responsibility is assigned to the countries extracting fossil fuels. Japan provides a striking example: it ranks sixth in historical emissions when measured by the fuels burned within its borders, but falls to 34th under extraction-based accounting because it relies heavily on imported fossil fuels.Population size also affects how historical responsibility is understood. Carbon Brief's analysis found that smaller countries exporting large quantities of oil and gas, including Brunei, Kuwait, Qatar, Norway and Trinidad and Tobago, rank prominently when extraction-based emissions are measured per person. This offers another perspective on the relationship between fossil fuel production, exports and historical climate impact.The dataset has some important limitations. Emissions are allocated according to present-day national borders, with historical production from the former Soviet Union, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia distributed among their successor countries using their shares at the time of separation. Carbon Brief describes the dataset as a draft release based on available information. Its results should therefore be understood as an alternative accounting framework rather than a definitive measure of legal responsibility.Who should pay for climate damage caused by exported fossil fuels?The findings have implications for international discussions about climate finance and the responsibility of fossil fuel-producing nations. Campaigners argue that countries that have earned substantial revenues from exporting coal, oil and gas should contribute more towards climate action and the costs of climate damage. At COP31, the debate has become particularly relevant because Australia is helping lead negotiations while continuing to export fossil fuels.The question is contested, though. A representative for the Saudi ministry of energy told The Guardian that it would be misleading to assign responsibility for emissions from exported oil solely to the producing country, arguing that importing nations decide how fuels are used and what technologies burn them. The representative also pointed to Saudi Arabia's efforts to reduce emissions from its own energy production. Robbie Andrew, whose data underpin the analysis, similarly told Carbon Brief that responsibility is shared between those who extract fossil fuels, those who produce and supply them, and those who consume them.The debate is not simply about which country appears highest on an emissions chart. It concerns how responsibility should be divided between fossil fuel exporters and the economies that have depended on their supplies. By adding the emissions from exported fuels to the picture, the analysis makes the historical role of energy producers more visible and raises further questions about who should fund the transition away from fossil fuels and help countries cope with climate change.You use AI every day. articles.title: Harrison Ford presents major conservation award to Mozambique’s Gorongosa Restoration Project, which rebuilt wildlife populations after more than 90% of large animals were lost during the civil war
articles.summary: Actor Harrison Ford has passed the E.O.
articles.body: Actor Harrison Ford has passed the E.O. Wilson Legacy Award for Transformative Conservation Leadership to Mozambique’s Gorongosa Restoration Project, recognising its efforts to rebuild a national park that lost more than 90% of its large animals during the civil war and its aftermath. The project, which began in 2008, has helped restore wildlife populations, with the park now holding more than 100% of its equivalent 1960s wildlife biomass and more than 250 lions. The award was presented at Harvard’s Sanders Theatre on October 12, 2026, with the project recognised for combining scientific research, biodiversity conservation and community development.How did Gorongosa rebuild its wildlife after the civil warGorongosa National Park, located in Mozambique, experienced a devastating decline in its wildlife population between 1972 and 2000, when more than 90% of its large animals were lost during the civil war and its aftermath. The restoration effort began in 2008 under a public-private partnership between the Government of Mozambique and the Carr Foundation, led by Greg Carr. The initiative has focused on rebuilding the park's wildlife populations while supporting the communities living around it.The foundation said the park now has more than 100% of the equivalent biomass of wildlife it had in the 1960s. Its lion population, which had fallen to single digits in 2004, has since grown to more than 250. The restoration was led by a combination of conservation science, habitat management and community programmes. Carr has devoted more than 20 years to the project, with an emphasis on ensuring that Mozambicans play a central role in the park's recovery.What has research revealed about Gorongosa's biodiversityScientific research has been central to the Gorongosa Restoration Project, which has partnered with more than 80 universities, including Harvard, Princeton, Stanford, Oxford and Cambridge. According to the E.O. Wilson Biodiversity Foundation, researchers have documented more than 8,000 species across the Greater Gorongosa landscape, with roughly 200 of them new to science. Research connected to the park has also produced more than 100 peer-reviewed articles, including findings on how decades of ivory poaching contributed to the rise of tuskless elephants.The park is also home to the only Master's programme in Conservation Biology conducted entirely inside a national park, according to the foundation. Forty-eight Mozambican students have graduated from the programme, with alumni going on to work in national parks, universities and government institutions. Six members of the park's staff also hold competitive PhD scholarships at universities in the United Kingdom, Portugal and South Africa. A survey conducted in July 2026 by a team led by Dr Jacinto Mathe documented approximately 592 plant, animal and fungal taxa over 11 days. Of these, 48 had never previously been recorded in the park, including what appeared to be a dung beetle new to science.What is Gorongosa doing to improve lives around the national parkThe Gorongosa Restoration Project has also worked to support communities living near the national park, following a One Health philosophy that recognises the connections between human health, wildlife and the environment. Its programmes include education, healthcare, forestry and agriculture initiatives designed to support local communities alongside wildlife conservation. In 2025, the project organised 353 mobile health clinics that reached more than 160,000 people, while 28 new schools were completed to serve 15,000 students.The same year, the project also planted more than 355,000 indigenous trees across 312 hectares. These initiatives formed part of the foundation's recognition of Gorongosa's wider conservation work, which combines the recovery of wildlife with community development. In 2025, the Gorongosa Restoration Project received the BBVA Foundation Worldwide Award for Biodiversity Conservation in recognition of its achievements over 20 years. Aurora Malene said: “Perhaps the greatest measure of restoration is not only what we bring back. It is what we make possible.”What is the E.O. Wilson Legacy Award and why was it createdThe E.O. Wilson Legacy Award for Transformative Conservation Leadership was established by the E.O. Wilson Biodiversity Foundation in 2025. It recognises individuals and organisations that advance the vision of the late biologist E.O. Wilson through scientific research, public engagement and efforts to encourage wider conservation action. Wilson had a longstanding connection with Gorongosa, having visited the park three times after learning about its restoration agreement in 2008.During his visits, Wilson recorded more than 200 ant species, including 20 that were new to science. He also wrote about the park in his 2014 book, A Window on Eternity, and the research centre at Chitengo was named the E.O. Wilson Biodiversity Laboratory in his honour. The foundation said the award was designed by sculptor and coin designer Heidi Wastweet and cast in bronze. Its central thumbprint represents the impact of human activity on the natural world, while a great blue heron symbolises natural wisdom and resilience. Three leaf-cutter ants along the base pay tribute to Wilson's research on ants. The award was presented during Half-Earth Day 2026, which also marked 10 years since Wilson launched the Half-Earth movement, calling for the protection of half the planet's land and sea for the rest of life.You use AI every day. articles.title: Postcard written by Titanic hero from Godalming sells for £32k
articles.summary: Wireless operator Jack Phillips, from Surrey, wrote the card when the ship was at Southampton.
articles.body:
A postcard written by the Titanic's senior wireless operator has sold for £32,000 at auction, well over the expected price of up to £20,000.

Jack Phillips, 25, who came from Surrey, wrote the card to his sister Elsie who lived in Godalming, while the ship was docked in Southampton on 6 April 1912.

Phillips, who died in the disaster alongside about 1,500 others, remained at his post sending wireless distress calls after the TItanic had struck an iceberg.

His postcard, which was among the lots at auction on Saturday in Wiltshire, reads: "Thanks very much for your letter. Having glorious weather, went to Cowes yesterday. Will write later before we sail."

Phillips was described by auctioneer Andrew Aldridge, of Henry Aldridge and Son Ltd in Devizes, as "one of the true heroes of the disaster".

He said: "After abandoning ship when water flooded around his feet, he ended up on an overturned collapsible lifeboat where he later died of exposure to the severe cold."

While more than 1,500 people died in the Titanic, 705 people were rescued on to the RMS Carpathia, which was sent thanks to Phillips' messages.

The wireless operator had learned Morse code while working in his first job at his local Post Office.

articles.title: 'Lotus has withered': Akhilesh Yadav's swipe at BJP over 'Radhe Radhe Kamal Khila De' slogan
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Taking a swipe at the BJP over its “Radhe Radhe Kamal Khila De” slogan for the upcoming Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, Samajwadi Party (SP)
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Taking a swipe at the BJP over its “Radhe Radhe Kamal Khila De” slogan for the upcoming Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav said on Sunday that the slogan itself indicated that the ruling party’s "kamal" (lotus symbol) had withered and needed to bloom once again."'Radhe Radhe Kamal Khila De' go ahead and make it bloom. Does it mean the lotus has withered? Why do you (BJP) need to make it bloom again? It has withered," the former Uttar Pradesh chief minister told reporters at a press conference in Lucknow.Akhilesh Yadav also accused the BJP of selectively invoking religious sentiments, clarifying that his party had no objection to religious discourses or 'kathas' but opposed controversial remarks about Hindu deities."The Samajwadi Party is not against 'katha'. But what were the views expressed about the father of Lord Shri Ram, and what was said about Lord Krishna? These are the same BJP people who once made Lord Hanuman dance at their programme," he said, without naming anyone."Can anyone make such remarks about Lord Ram's father? Tell me, what would happen if someone from among us made a similar statement?" he added.Although the SP chief did not name anyone, his remarks appeared to be directed at preacher Dhirendra Krishna Shastri, who recently courted controversy over statements concerning Lord Ram and Lord Krishna.Akhilesh Yadav also hit back at Uttar Pradesh deputy chief minister and BJP leader Keshav Prasad Maurya over his remarks that SP leaders, who once hesitated to chant "Jai Shri Ram", were now uncomfortable with the slogan "Radhe Radhe".Responding to Maurya's comments, Akhilesh Yadav said, "I would never invite him (Maurya) to my house in my lifetime. But you are welcome to visit our house; we will greet you with 'Radhe Radhe'," he told a reporter.The Uttar Pradesh assembly elections are scheduled to take place in February-March next year. The BJP will be aiming for a third consecutive term in power, while Akhilesh Yadav will look to become chief minister for a second time, having last held the post from 2012 to 2017.(With PTI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A diamond ring worn by Titanic survivor Lucy, Lady Duff Gordon when the ship sank in 1912 remained in her family for generations; on November 21 it sold for £150,000, nearly twice its £80,000 auction estimate
articles.summary: A remarkable diamond ring worn by Titanic survivor Lucy, Lady Duff Gordon, sold for £150,000, almost double its auction estimate, highlighting its historical significance and familial legacy.
articles.body: A diamond ring worn by Titanic survivor Lucy, Lady Duff Gordon, when the passenger liner sank in 1912 has sold for £150,000, nearly twice its pre-auction estimate, after remaining with her family for generations.The solitaire diamond ring was sold on Saturday at Henry Aldridge & Son in Devizes, Wiltshire. It had been expected to fetch around £80,000, but the final price reached £150,000, The Independent reported.Lady Duff Gordon was wearing the ring when the Titanic sank during its maiden voyage on April 15, 1912, claiming around 1,500 lives. The jewellery became a significant family heirloom and was known among her descendants as the 'Titanic Ring'. It was also believed to have been her engagement ring.The ring was the only piece of jewellery of significance belonging to Lady Duff Gordon that survived the disaster. It was later passed down through her family, eventually reaching her grandson, John, the 3rd Earl of Halsbury, a British crossbench peer and scientist.Following his death, the ring remained with the family, which continued to preserve it across generations. Its eventual sale offered collectors an opportunity to acquire a personal possession connected to one of the Titanic's best-known survivors.Andrew Aldridge of Henry Aldridge & Son highlighted the rarity of the item coming to auction through the survivor's direct descendants.“It’s exceptionally rare for jewellery related to a Titanic survivor to come to market but almost unprecedented for such a personal item from such a high-profile passenger to be sold at auction via direct descent,” Aldridge said.How Lady Duff Gordon escaped the Titanic sinkingLady Duff Gordon travelled to the United States with her husband, Sir Cosmo Duff Gordon, aboard the Titanic as a first-class passenger in 1912. Their secretary, Laura Mabel Francatelli, was also travelling with them.All three escaped aboard Lifeboat No 1 during the evacuation. Although the boat had capacity for 40 people, it was lowered with just 12 occupants, including seven crew members.After being rescued by the RMS Carpathia, the Cunard liner that picked up survivors, Sir Cosmo gave each of the men from their lifeboat a cheque for £5. The money was intended to compensate them after the White Star Line stopped paying their wages following the sinking.The payments subsequently became the subject of controversy, with rumours that the Duff Gordons had bribed the crew not to return to the sinking ship to rescue people in the water, fearing that additional passengers could overwhelm the lifeboat.Other Titanic memorabilia sold at the auctionThe sale also featured other items connected to the ship and its final voyage, including a rare ticket that allowed visitors to view the Titanic before it departed Southampton.The day ticket sold for £40,000. Dated April 10, 1912, it carried the White Star burgee and was addressed to the officer in charge. It included the instruction: “Please allow Mr Talbot and 2 friends to view the S.S. Titanic.”A handwritten note on its reverse read: “Mrs Dibden plus two sisters.”The ticket belonged to Eliza Dibden, who took it aboard the ship. She was the mother of William Dibden, an 18-year-old from the New Forest in Hampshire who died in the disaster. His first communion certificate, dated Easter 1908, was also included with the ticket.Another item from the auction was a postcard written by Titanic's senior wireless operator, Jack Phillips, which fetched £32,000.Phillips, who was 25, sent the postcard to his sister, Elsie Phillips, on April 6, 1912, while the Titanic was docked in Southampton. The front featured a photograph of the liner, while the message referred to his recent visit to Cowes and the good weather before the ship's departure.“Thanks very much for your letter. Having glorious weather, went to Cowes yesterday. Will write later before we sail,” he wrote.Phillips later sent wireless messages requesting assistance from other ships as the Titanic sank, helping efforts to rescue passengers and crew. Aldridge described him as “one of the true heroes of the disaster”.The auction totals, including the £150,000 achieved by Lady Duff Gordon's ring, include the buyer's premium.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Wisconsin woman bought a 1900 Victorian home for $614,000 in 2020, painted it dark for a Gothic theme, and later turned it into a pink ‘Barbie Dream House’ rental; it is now under contract after a $1.1 million listing
articles.summary: Ever dreamed of living in a Barbie house IRL? Well, someone may have beaten you to it.
articles.body: Ever dreamed of living in a Barbie house IRL? Well, someone may have beaten you to it. A pink Victorian ‘Barbie Dream House’ in Hudson, Wisconsin, has gone under contract after being listed for $1.1 million. The seven-bedroom house, originally built in 1900, has had many personas before transforming into an all-pink Barbiecore castle. From the bubblegum walls to its pink staircase, many people have called it a ‘Barbie Dream House’. After entering the market in June this year, the property has now gone under contract, according to a report by Realtor.com.From Goth mansion to Barbie houseThe house at 1031 2nd St. in Hudson, Wisconsin, did not always look like a playhouse. The current seller bought the property in 2020 for $614,000. After purchasing it, the owner painted it black, according to Jennifer R. Martin, the listing agent with Edina Realty. “When the seller bought it, right away she had it painted in dark charcoal. Her vision at that time was to have a Goth mansion that would be similar to Disney’s Haunted Mansion. It was right around the time the 'Barbie' movie was coming out, so she decided to take advantage of that,” Martin told the outlet. The seller repainted the house in a custom pink shortly before the Barbie movie reached theatres that summer. “It was my dream to have a pink house, and so I made that dream a reality. And here we are. I love the colour. It's very vibrant. It means love. It's very girly,” homeowner Brooke Fleetwood told CBS News.Talking about the transformation from Goth mansion to Barbie house, she said, “It started out with being a black, Gothic house. Very dark, sexy vibes. And then I changed it about a month, month and a half ago to the Barbiecore Castle.”A Barbie-themed rentalAfter painting it pink, the owner transformed it into a short-term rental. The property hosted birthday parties, bachelorette weekends and other group stays. “The seller’s clientele is looking for a party weekend destination. It’s one block from the riverfront and two blocks away from downtown,” Martin said.The property sits near the St Croix River, about one block from the riverfront and two blocks from downtown. Hudson lies about 30 miles east of Minneapolis, and Minneapolis–St Paul International Airport is roughly 30 minutes away. Guests can walk to boutique shops, riverfront parks and the marina.Inside the pink houseIf you are a fan of pink, you may be surprised by the variety of shades used throughout the property. The pink walls, drapes and couches are a sight for sore eyes. Spanning 5,189 sq ft across multiple levels, the house has seven bedrooms and four bathrooms. It also features two full kitchens, formal and informal dining spaces, expansive gathering areas, original woodwork, built-in cabinetry, fireplaces and two stunning statement staircases. Four bedrooms are on the second level, along with three additional bedrooms on the third level. There is also a dedicated movie room and a spacious owner's suite complete with an en-suite bathroom, walk-in wardrobe and laundry facilities. Other features include a home theatre, a hot tub, a 14-foot swim spa and a patio built for entertaining. The fenced lot has a two-car garage and a driveway that can accommodate 12 vehicles.According to the listing agent, the house could suit a multigenerational family or be converted back into a single-family home. “The sizing alone of the house is incredible. It’s enormous and goes on forever. It has two separate kitchens, so it could also be turned into a duplex,” she said.The listing also highlights the property's potential for different uses: “The property offers multiple value-add opportunities. It can continue operating as a high-demand vacation rental, serve as your flagship addition to an investment portfolio, easily be configured as a duplex with a separate apartment space ready for additional rental income, or be converted into a remarkable single-family residence.”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Why have UN efforts to regulate ‘killer robots’ stalled?
articles.summary: CWC countries agree to ‘elaborate’ on potential accord regulating autonomous weapons in two years, prompting criticism.
articles.body:
A United Nations conference has failed to agree on the swift adoption of legally binding rules to regulate autonomous weapon systems known as “killer robots”.

The member states of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) met in Switzerland this week to discuss developing a new treaty which would regulate how the systems are used amid growing alarm over artificial intelligence (AI)-driven warfare and the lack of transparency and accountability.

But on Saturday, participants fell short of securing a mandate to negotiate a legally binding ban, agreeing instead to “elaborate” on a potential accord regulating such weapon systems by 2028. Rights groups and NGOs called the development “disappointing”.

According to the UN, lethal autonomous weapons systems are “a combination of one or more weapons and technological components operating together, that is capable of identifying, selecting, and engaging a target in a way that results in loss of life, without intervention by a human being operating the system”.

In simpler terms, they are systems that can identify, select and engage a target without human intervention. They are commonly referred to as “killer robots”, but this is not an established technical or legal designation.

The systems are programmed with a specific “target profile” before deployment, using sensor data such as facial recognition and other technologies to search for and kill matching targets.

“When the weapon encounters someone or something the algorithm perceives to match its target profile, it fires and kills,” the Autonomous Weapons Organisation explains.

According to the UN, not all autonomous weapon systems use AI. At the same time, AI is not necessary for autonomous weapon systems to function, nor does it determine whether a system is autonomous.

“However, when AI is used to identify, select and engage targets, it can amplify the serious legal, ethical, humanitarian and security concerns associated with autonomous weapon systems,” the UN warns.

Despite the concerns, AI-assisted weapons have already been used in the wars in Ukraine and Sudan and conflicts in the Middle East. Israel has used surveillance tools and AI-powered targeting systems in its genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.

Adopted in 1980, the CCW was established as a key international humanitarian law instrument.

“Its purpose is to ban or restrict the use of specific types of weapons that are considered to cause unnecessary or unjustifiable suffering to combatants or to affect civilians indiscriminately,” the UN says.

There is currently no legally binding instrument under the CCW that specifically regulates autonomous weapon systems.

The 128 countries that are party to the CCW met in the Swiss city of Geneva to discuss whether to authorise negotiations on curbs and a potential ban on such systems.

Julien Thoeni, the Swiss diplomat who chaired the Geneva conference, said the process should determine which weapons can be banned under international humanitarian law and which can be permitted but regulated.

The week-long conference came after nearly 100 countries agreed last month that it was important to swiftly adopt legally binding rules on the weapons capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.

But on Saturday, key arms-producing nations, including the United States, Russia and Israel, opposed the push. Decisions under the convention require the agreement of all member states.

Diplomats told the Reuters news agency that negotiations over the final wording of the treaty had continued all night after Russian objections to rules of procedure forced the cancellation of some formal meetings.

Two EU diplomats told media outlet Politico that the US, the UK, South Korea, Japan, Turkiye and Israel were also countries that resisted an effort to agree on a binding regulation. Others supporting a new convention included the European Union and NATO member states, as well as Ukraine, China and Iran, diplomats cited by The Guardian newspaper said.

In the end, all countries agreed on a watered-down convention which aims to develop new rules to regulate such weapons by 2028.

A diplomat involved in the talks from a country supporting the new laws told Reuters that the outcome was “disappointing but could have been much worse”.

Why did some resist regulating ‘killer robots’?

While most countries support a pact to regulate “killer robots”, major military powers are opposing it, saying that humanitarian law linked to those weapons is sufficient.

As investment in AI warfare and autonomous systems grows, those countries also resist restrictions that could curb their ability to develop, test or use advanced weapons on modern battlefields. So rather than committing to strict legal obligations, they favour flexible, non-binding frameworks or longer timelines for discussions.

Swiss diplomat Thoeni told reporters after the meeting ended that some countries had rejected the word “negotiate”. The agreed text refers instead to the “elaboration” of an instrument.

Stop Killer Robots, a coalition of some 300 organisations opposed to the development and use of autonomous weapons, called the mandate “watered down” and said it offered no clear route to legally binding rules.

Its executive director, Nicole van Rooijen, said autonomous weapons were being deployed in combat, including systems that use artificial intelligence to choose targets.

“Delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” she told AFP news agency.

Critics also warned that without a binding treaty, the weapons objectify people and undermine their dignity by reducing human lives to sensor data and algorithmic targets.

Georgia Hinds, legal adviser at the International Committee of the Red Cross, said that “there is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm”.

“That’s not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross,” Hinds added.
